item.title: [Field Level Media] Brewers turn to Jacob Misiorowski in 2nd attempt to end World Series

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — With some pent-up energy and a fearless attitude, the Tampa Bay Rays extended their season at least one more day and will play host to Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday.
With the Rays down to their last three outs, Jonny DeLuca and Ben Williamson provided the heroics to alter the narrative after Tampa Bay had been stymied at every turn over the first three games by the Milwaukee Brewers.
After falling into a 3-0 series hole, the Rays will now try to lean into their new-found momentum, but first they need to come up with a pitching plan.
Tampa Bay right-hander Nick Martinez would have been the probable Game 5 starter, but he was needed to pitch two innings on Tuesday.
“We’re going to get together after this session and sit down and talk about pitching,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after the victory. “Going to check who’s available. I’m going to guess most guys are going to say they’re capable of an inning or more given it’s Game 5 of the World Series, but nothing has been decided yet.”
The Brewers tied the Tuesday game 2-2 in the fifth inning on a home run from David Hamilton, and the score remained even until the 12th when Cooper Pratt hit a home run for Milwaukee.
Down 3-2, Tampa Bay caught a rare break when Brewers third baseman Joey Ortiz committed a throwing error on Junior Caminero’s grounder to open the bottom of the 12th. Liam Hicks singled before DeLuca delivered an RBI single to center to tie the game 3-all.
After a Chandler Simpson single loaded the bases with no outs, Williamson came on to pinch-hit and bounced a ball into right field to set off a Rays celebration on the infield.
“Cash just kind of turned around and said, ‘Get ready to hit,'” Williamson said. “Jokingly in my head, I was thinking, ‘Yeah, I’ve been ready to hit since the fourth or fifth inning.'”
The Brewers now have one more opportunity to clinch their first-ever World Series title on the road, then would play host to Games 6 and 7, if necessary.
“Nobody said any of this was going to be easy, but I think we have the right group to get a good night’s sleep, flush it and be ready to go (Wednesday),” said Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers, who is 2-for-17 with three walks in the series after winning the National League Championship Series MVP award.
While Tampa Bay scrambles to put together a pitching plan, Milwaukee will send NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski to the mound. The hard-throwing right-hander allowed one run over five innings to earn the win in Game 1.
In three starts and 13 1/3 innings this postseason, Misiorowski is 1-0 with a 2.70 ERA and 14 strikeouts, although he had just three against the Rays in the series opener.
“You can write it up and hope that they perform like the back of their baseball card, but that doesn’t always happen,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after announcing Misiorowski as his starter. “You go with what you believe is the deal. I trust our guys. They put themselves in a position to win.”
While the Rays used seven pitchers to keep their season alive in Game 4, the Brewers went even deeper by using eight in an unsuccessful attempt to close out their first-ever World Series championship. Game 5 could come down to which bullpen bounces back best.
“You’re seeing two elite contact offenses where strikeouts are very tough to come by,” Cash said. “We weren’t knocking balls in the gap or knocking balls out of the ballpark. We pieced together a big (12th inning), maybe the most important inning of our season.”
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Happy Monday, everyone! The World Series got underway this weekend, and it hasn’t felt particularly close at all so far. While the Rays did take an early lead in Game 2, they seemed to drop the ball (literally) after the first inning with lacklustre defense and silent bats. The Brewers now have a 2-0 series lead as the games head to St. Petersburg for the week, so we’ll see if the Rays have another series comeback in them.
We have a lot about the World Series below, plus some Blue Jays insight, and Stephen Vogt shooting down rumors that he might be leaving Cleveland. So let’s just jump right into it.
- Michael Baumann looks at what’s been working (and not working) for the Brewers and Rays so far.
- Ben Clemens checks in on the unlikely hero who helped push the Brewers to a 2-0 series lead.
- Adam Berry offers three ways the Rays can come back and force the series to return to Milwaukee.
- Ranking all 52 players in the World Series. (SI)
- Rob Manfred says a small-market World Series is good for baseball, but a salary cap is still necessary. Story by Jesse Rogers.
- Jacob Misiorowski threw the fastest pitch in World Series history this weekend. (AP)
- Kiley McDaniel thinks players like Jackson Chourio and Junior Caminero bring much-needed excitement to the postseason.
- Ken Rosenthal looks at how the Rays seem to be falling apart in the World Series. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Wisconsin has money to burn, it seems.
- Matthew Roberson takes a look at some of the terrible defense we saw in Game Two of the World Series.
- Anthony DiComo has some key takeaways from Game Two.
- Adam McCalvy spotlights the Brewers fan who walks to every single home game.
- Tom Verducci looks at how Aaron Ashby has played it cool and come in very handy for the Brewers this postseason.
- Tim Kurkjian compares the 2026 Brewers to the 1982 Brewers.
- Cody Stavenhagen shares how the memory of Bob Uecker is making this Brewers postseason a bittersweet one. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Things to love this postseason: Payton Tolle as a correspondent.
- Jon Becker delivers a postseason report card for Stephen Vogt.
- Jared Greenspan looks at the major velocity jump taken by Freddy Peralta this offseason.
- Keegan Matheson determines how returning injured players could impact the Blue Jays’ offseason plans.
- Bryan Hoch spotlights the Rays’ clubhouse attendant who helped make a custom glove for a Buccaneers player.
- Stephen Vogt insisted Mariners interview rumors at hokum and he will return to the Guardians next season. (AP)
- Grant Brisbee ranks the worst commercials of the MLB postseason. (The Athletic subscription required.)
- Can’t say this was on my bingo card…
And tomorrow will be a better day than today, Buster. Make it so.

item.content:encoded:
La espera de los fanáticos por el estreno de la nueva entrega de Avengers: Doomsday es más llevadera ahora, debido a que el mexicano Randy Arozarena participó en uno de los videos promocionales más recientes: donde funge como uno de los protagonistas junto a sus múltiples estrellas de las Grandes Ligas.
El pelotero de Seattle Mariners, que será agente libre al término de la campaña, se ha convertido en una de las figuras más queridas dentro de la Major League Baseball (MLB). Además de deslumbrar en Estados Unidos, ha brillado en el diamante por sus participaciones con la Selección Mexicana.
La franquicia de Marvel ha marcado varios momentos en lo deportivo, ya que en la Liga MX ha coincidido de manera sorprendente con que Santos Laguna se convierta en el campeón del futbol mexicano: motivo por el que la afición está ilusionada esta campaña con los Guerreros.
Randy Arozarena aparece en Avengers: Doomsday
A menos de dos meses de que se estrene Avengers: Doomsday en cines, Randy Arozarena aparece como uno de los jugadores de la MLB elegidos para promocionar la cinta, donde se le ve al mexicano hablar con Freddie Freeman, Bryce Harper, Jacob Misiorowski y Junior Caminero sobre el lanzamiento inicial a cargo de los Cuatro Fantásticos.
También te puede interesar: Exatlón México: ¿Por qué habría 2 expulsados HOY 25 de octubre? Esta sería la razón | Spoilers
Los beisbolistas señalan en tono de sátira que el espectáculo inicial es cada vez más grande, a lo que Arozarena pregunta “quién sigue, ¿los Vengadores?”, mientras pasan escenas del filme, hasta que llega el clímax donde el Dr. Doom aterriza en el diamante; por lo que deciden marcharse del lugar.
¿Cómo va la Serie Mundial entre Rayas y Cerveceros?
Hasta este domingo, la Serie Mundial de la MLB se mantiene con los Cerveceros de Milwaukee arriba por 2-0 sobre las Rayas de Tampa Bay: antiguo equipo del mexicano de 31 años, donde el juego del sábado terminó muy cerrado con un marcador de 5-4 a favor de los Brewers.
El siguiente compromiso de la gran final de las Grandes Ligas se llevará a cabo este lunes 26 de octubre de 2026, en punto de las 18:00 horas, tiempo del Centro de México, en el diamante del Tropicana Field de San Petersburgo, en el que buscarán ampliar su ventaja en la serie.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski's pre-Game 2 routine? Trading Pokémon cards with fans appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Manager Pat Murphy's Milwaukee Brewers made history in Game 1 of the World Series, scoring a win over the Tampa Bay Rays by a score of 3-2 behind ace hurler Jacob Misiorowski. The Brewers planned to send Logan Henderson to the mound for Game 2 giving Misiorowski a chance to relax beforehand.
The Brewers star was spotted near the dugout, as shared by MLB Network's Jon Heyman, as he began trading Pokemon cards with a young fan.
Misiorowski has become a favorite player for fans of all ages as he has led the Brewers to huge win after huge win, including a sweep over the back-to-back defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS. Misiorowski made World Series history on his first pitch of Game 1, scorching the radar gun with a fastball that looked like something out of a Disney movie.
The Brewers' starting pitching was seen as lacking depth compared to the Rays heading into the World Series, but Misiorwoski did his job, giving way to Henderson for Game 2 at American Family Field in Milwaukee. Henderson has compiled statistics in recent games that have given the Brewers confidence that he can lead his team to victory.
The Brewers' home ballpark can hold nearly 42,000 fans, and they appear united behind their team in pursuit of their first-ever World Series championship. Misiorowski might not get the chance to pitch for Murphy's team for a few games, but he is clearly making the most of his time in the fall classic as fans continue to enjoy the ride headed deep into October.
Related: Former MVP Ryan Braun gets completely real on Brewers' World Series vs. Rays

item.title: [FanSided] How Jacob Misiorowski was almost a Rays ace, flipping the World Series upside down
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman

item.content:encoded:
At some point during Friday’s World Series opener, we’re sure plenty of Tampa Bay Rays fans wished they had their own version of Jacob Misiorowski.
As it turns out, the Rays may have been among those legitimately interested in having the real thing.
Social media is far more efficient than people give it credit for, and a July 2025 article regarding the Brewers’ ace resurfaced on Friday morning. Major League Baseball’s Adam McCalvy reported last year that the Rays, Brewers and Rockies were the only three MLB teams that attended a December 2019 bullpen session in Kansas City to see the Miz, who at that point was in his senior year of high school and far lighter than his current 6-foot-7, 201-pound frame.
“I don’t know if I’ve ever written a report on a guy off one bullpen with that conviction,” Brewers regional scouting supervisor Drew Anderson said.
Misiorowski lost his senior season to the pandemic and enrolled at Crowder College (Mo.) after going undrafted. Milwaukee instead used a second-round pick on the future All-Star in 2022 — two spots ahead of Tampa, who took outfielder Brock Jones instead.
What would have happened had the Tampa Bay Rays drafted Jacob Misiorowski?
Whether it’s JaMarcus Russell or Greg Oden, sports fans love a good “what if?” discussion. We’re too early in Misiorowski’s career to fully evaluate and predict a world in which he landed in Tampa Bay instead of Milwaukee.
What we found interesting is that some in the Brewers’ 2020 draft room fought for Misiorowski and suggested paying him third-round money. But because the pandemic shortened the draft to five rounds, they felt they shouldn’t take the risk — which, for the record, we agree was the right call given the context.
But should the Rays have possibly taken the opposite approach and selected Misiorowski in 2020? Those questions are notoriously difficult in baseball; it’s easy to forget he was an 18-year-old who hadn’t pitched a meaningful game in over a year. We don’t know how he’d have fared without three years of experience — albeit temporarily halted by a freshman-year knee injury — in college and summer ball.
Anderson referenced Pirates ace Paul Skenes, who went No. 1 in 2023, and how easy a decision that was for Pittsburgh. Milwaukee lucked out, so to speak, by having an incredible player development program that consistently churns out above-average position players and reliable pitchers. Imagine if Misiorowski landed in Colorado?
Misiorowski did his part on Friday night, limiting the Rays to one run over five innings. Assuming the Brewers hold on and win their first World Series title, we hope Anderson and area scout Riley Bandelow receive better treatment than the New York Knicks’ employees.

item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers won Game 1 of the World Series behind a solid start from Jacob Misiorowski. He went five innings and picked up the win.
It was Misiorowski's longest start of the postseason, and he was the Brewers' first starting pitcher to get a win in the postseason. The 24-year-old is poised to win the National League Cy Young Award in the coming weeks, and on Friday, he became the youngest starting pitcher since Jaret Wright to get a win in Game 1 of the World Series.
Wright's win came in 1997 when Cleveland played the Florida Marlins. He was 21 years old at the time.
It really puts into perspective how hard it is to pitch well on the biggest stage as a young pitcher. Misiorowski has been lighting up the radar gun this October, but he has been nowhere near as dominant as he was in the regular season.
The Brewers threw their best arm in Game 1, but the Tampa Bay Rays did not. Misiorowski will be lined up to pitch in Game 5, while Drew Rasmussen looks like he will pitch in Game 2 and Game 6, should the series get there.
However,. depending on how the series goes, the Brewers and Rays could both move where their aces are slated to pitch.

item.content:encoded:
Marvel Studios a trouvé un endroit inattendu pour montrer de nouvelles images d’Avengers : Doomsday : une coupure publicitaire des World Series, la finale du championnat nord-américain de baseball. Le spot est passé sur Fox ce vendredi 23 octobre, pendant le premier match entre les Brewers de Milwaukee et les Rays de Tampa Bay. En France, c’était dans la nuit de vendredi à samedi.
Pour les fans, ces images arrivent à moins de deux mois de la sortie, prévue le mercredi 16 décembre 2026 en France, deux jours avant les États-Unis. Elles s’ajoutent à la première bande-annonce, publiée le 20 juillet, et à la deuxième, dévoilée en août à la D23, la convention de fans de Disney. En revanche, elles ne révèlent rien de majeur sur l’intrigue.
Que montre le nouveau teaser d’Avengers : Doomsday ?
Ce spot joue à fond la carte du baseball. On retrouve les Quatre Fantastiques à Ebbets Field, l’ancien stade des Dodgers de Brooklyn, démoli en 1960 dans notre monde mais toujours debout dans le film.
Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) y utilise son bras élastique pour lancer la première balle du match (c’est de la triche, non ?). Cinq joueurs de la MLB, la ligue nord-américaine de baseball, s’invitent aussi sur le banc : Bryce Harper (Phillies), Freddie Freeman (Dodgers), Randy Arozarena (Mariners), Junior Caminero (Rays) et Jacob Misiorowski, lanceur partant des Brewers pendant ce même premier match. Selon la MLB, la scène est bien tirée du film, mais les joueurs y ont été ajoutés pour ce spot.
Au milieu de ces images, Marvel s’amuse surtout de la présence de ses deux Captain America. Scott Lang, alias Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), appelle spontanément Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) « Cap », avant de se reprendre : le titre revient désormais à Sam Wilson (Anthony Mackie). Cette petite hésitation donne un aperçu des échanges que pourrait provoquer le retour de Steve, qui avait transmis son bouclier à Sam à la fin d’Avengers : Endgame.
Thor et Black Panther apparaissent également, tandis que Doctor Doom clôt la vidéo, toujours dissimulé sous son masque et sa capuche. Marvel montre ainsi ses héros et son méchant, sans rien dévoiler de ce qui les attend.

item.title: [trentonian.com] World Series: Brewers withstand Rays’ comeback attempt to win Game 1
item.dc:creator: Steve Megargee

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Trevor Megill was shouting in celebration and the Milwaukee Brewers were bolting out of the dugout to congratulate one another, believing they had just escaped a ninth-inning jam to win Game 1 of the World Series.
Not quite yet.
What initially was ruled a game-ending double play got overturned after a video review showed Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
No problem.
Megill regrouped and struck out Jonny DeLuca with two runners in scoring position as Milwaukee edged the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 on Friday night.
“It’s good to get the first win out of the way,” Megill said. “That’s where all the nerves are at. First game, a lot of anticipation and build-up to where we are right now.”
The ninth inning was particularly nerve-racking for the Brewers and the sellout crowd attending Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982.
“You have a big range of emotions,” said team captain Christian Yelich, whose RBI triple in the first put the Brewers ahead for good. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn’t put a runner on since the sixth until it mounted its comeback attempt against Megill.
Jonathan Aranda, who went 3 for 3 with a walk, and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put runners on second and third before Junior Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Liam Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was called a 4-6-3 double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared. But then the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
“You’ve got to think worst-case scenario there,” Megill said. “I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base. Zoomed in and it didn’t look good. It’s all right. We picked up Cooper there. He’ll pick us up tomorrow.”
The out call at second was changed to safe by umpire Alfonso Márquez at the MLB Replay Center, which caught Pratt by surprise.
“Obviously, it was close,” the 22-year-old rookie said. “I just didn’t think it was enough to overturn, so I wasn’t thinking anything of it. The video I saw, thought my cleat was dragging. … There must have been some other angles that I haven’t seen. It ultimately didn’t matter because we won.”
The Brewers won because Megill got DeLuca to swing and miss at a 2-2 pitch, capping a night in which Tampa Bay went 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position.
“This is an extremely confident group,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “You know that. We know that. They’re going to be fine. I think the frustration comes from we were one swing of the bat away right at the end of potentially taking the lead.”
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
Milwaukee took a 2-0 lead in the first inning against Nick Martinez. NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to help the Brewers stay in front before relievers Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby shut down the Rays through the eighth.
Misiorowski, who had a season-low three strikeouts, opened the game with a 103.5 mph fastball — the fastest pitch ever thrown in a World Series.
“The adrenaline kind of took over, and I tensed up and threw it hard,” said Misiorowski, who earned the win. “Then I settled down, and that was the game plan, to settle in and do me. Don’t try and overdo it.”
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
Tampa Bay managed to hang around thanks in part to Martinez, who gave up those two runs in the first but held Milwaukee scoreless through the rest of his five-inning stint. The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh when Chourio singled home Pratt.
Then came all the action in the ninth, with the Brewers’ premature celebration followed by a team-wide sigh of relief as Pratt offered some parting words to Megill.
“I just said, ‘Thank you, man. Thanks for picking me up,’” Pratt said. “That’s what this game is. It’s a game of pick-me-up. He picked me up today.”
Up next
Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA) pitches for Tampa Bay and Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47) starts for Milwaukee in Game 2 on Saturday night. In this postseason, Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA and Henderson is 0-0 with a 3.00 ERA.

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE – Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
Recommended Videos
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5 mph fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Díaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2 mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1 mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100 mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100 mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. But his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100 mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz's first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field couldn't keep up, flashing 103.4 mph — one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101 mph or higher, 11 of 102 mph or more and three at 103-plus mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he couldn't take in the introductions before Milwaukee's first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy," he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”
___

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski drops brutally honest admission on his Game 1 start appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Milwaukee Brewers possessed a top-notch bullpen in the regular season and in the last two rounds of the playoffs, but the idea of this team winning a championship without Jacob Misiorowski posting his best stuff seemed near-incomprehensible. The presumptive National League Cy Young was unable to reach the sixth inning for a third straight postseason start, and yet, the Brew Crew are now just three wins away from capturing their first World Series title in franchise history.
Misiorowski pitched five innings of one-run ball in Friday's 3-2 Game 1 victory versus the Tampa Bay Rays, allowing four hits while recording three strikeouts and one walk. He perfectly described his fairly short yet triumphant outing.
"Not perfect, good enough to get a win," the genial 24-year-old right-hander said, via Joey Mistretta of ClutchPoints.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Misiorowski has not been operating as a work horse for some time. He has accumulated only a combined 13 1/3 innings of work across three playoff outings. The three Ks are also surprisingly low. This record-breaking flamethrower is nearing the end of his first full MLB campaign, and he is showing the effects of unleashing elite velocity all yearlong.
Like Misiorowski said, though, he had enough on this night. The Brewers' bullpen also provided first-class reinforcements, once again. Aaron Ashby remains unstoppable, Abner Uribe enjoyed a stellar showing in his own right and Trevor Megill survived despite allowing one run in the ninth. The lineup notched timely hits, as it does, and All-Star catcher William Contreras threw out potential game-tying runs multiple times.
Jacob Misiorowski did not carry the squad to a 1-0 series lead in American Family Field. Pat Murphy has not asked him to fill that role during this postseason. Milwaukee secured the W by putting forth a complete effort. This ballclub may not have many household names, but it should be obvious by now that one player does not define Brewers baseball.
If Milwaukee has its way, Misiorowski will not have to put the team on his back again for the rest of 2026. Game 2 is Saturday at approximately 8 p.m. ET.
Related: Brewers' Aaron Ashby reveals how he found his postseason groove in 2026
Related: Watch Brewers fans celebrate 1st World Series game win in 44 years

item.content:encoded:
Why Rays' key to World Series victory might revolve around Jacob Misiorowski originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Tampa Bay Rays are facing the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 MLB World Series, and after the Brewers swept the reining champions in four games in the NLCS, the Brewers are favorites in this matchup.
They also have home-field advantage, which makes the Rays' task a lot harder. But there's certainly a path for the Rays to win it all. But how can they actually win the World Series?
ESPN's Alden Gonzalez highlighted how the Brewers have a vulnerable starting rotation, led by Jacob Misiorowski, and that if the Rays can chase him out of the game early, the Rays could be set up for a lot of success in the World Series.
Rays can beat Brewers by getting after Jacob Misiorowski
"To beat the Brewers, you have to take advantage of their starting rotation," Gonzalez writes. "It begins with running up the pitch counts of their two front-line starters, Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson."
If the Rays are able to make the Brewers' top-two starting pitchers throw a lot of pitches early in games, making it so they don't last long in their respective starts, they can have a real chance of winning it all.
It might seem like a simple thing to chase a pitcher early, but considering the Brewers' top-heavy bullpen, getting to the middle of the bullpen might prove to be a key to this series.
Besides, in Games 3 and 4, Milwaukee will be relying on more of their bullpen, with starters Dustin May, Shane Drohan, and Robert Gasser set to be involved.
If the Rays can force the Brewers to the bullpen early in Games 1 and 2, they could set themselves up nicely for the rest of the series.
As Gonzalez put it, "scoring early will be a must for the Rays." They can win the World Series even if they struggle against Misiorowski and Henderson, but if they have success against them, their odds of winning the series will increase significantly.
The snowball effect of chasing Misiorowski and/or Henderson from a game early would be huge. Taxing the Brewers' bullpen is the key to the Rays' success, and to do so, they're going to have to get after Misiorowski.
Games 1 and 2 might be a telling outcome for how the series will go. If the Rays can tax the bullpens, they could be set up for success once the series heads to Tampa Bay.
They'll need their own pitchers to play great, but if the Rays' offense can force the pitch counts of Henderson and Misiorowski to go high early in their respective starts, they could be set up for success in the World Series against the Brewers.

As someone who married into a family of Rays fans and will be in Florida with my wife’s family for Halloween I would love to say the Rays will win in seven and I will watch that game with her family, but it is hard to vote against the Brewers. item.content:encoded:
Another season is coming to a close – the World Series is here. The Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays, both vying for their first championship. Who do we think will win? In how many games? Who will get MVP? Here are our thoughts.
As someone who married into a family of Rays fans and will be in Florida with my wife’s family for Halloween I would love to say the Rays will win in seven and I will watch that game with her family, but it is hard to vote against the Brewers.
They have the better offense. They have the better starting pitching. They have the deeper bullpen. They may even be better defensively. And they are going to be a bit more rested.
Because I will be on an airplane for game six I will say that the Brewers will win in six games.
The fun WSMVP choice would be Aaron Ashby continuing to dominate and taking the award by storm but a reliever has not won the WSMVP since Mariano Rivera in 1999 and Ashby is not the team’s primary closer.
So I will go with Jacob Misiorowski throwing two elite starts in games one and five, as well as an impact relief appearance in game six.
I think these teams are pretty evenly matched – the Rays have the upper hand in starting pitching, the Brewers have the better bullpen. While the Brewers scored more runs in the regular season, the teams had similar rate stats (Milwaukee had a 105 OPS+, compared to Tampa Bay’s 103). The Rays’ starters have consistently worked deeper into games compared to Milwaukee, and I wonder at what point the wear and tear will start to get to the Brewers’ bullpen. The Rays don’t strike out often, which leads me to believe they can be the team that finally conquers Milwaukee’s relievers. Milwaukee’s offense was relentless against the Dodgers, so it won’t be easy for the Rays to keep the Brewers down.
Overall, I think this will be a hard-fought series, with the Rays emerging victorious in seven games. Drew Rasmussen will win World Series MVP, winning his starts in Game 1 and Game 5, then coming out of the bullpen to pitch in Game 7.
Brewers in 7, Jackson Chourio is MVP. I wish Bob Uecker was here to see it.
Brewers in six. This should be a really fun and competitive series between two teams who play baseball the right way. Pitching wins, especially in the postseason, so Jacob Misiorowski will win the MVP after authoring his postseason legacy with two elite starts and a gutsy appearance out of the bullpen with everything on the line.
Brewers in 6. Christian Yelich wins MVP as he lives up to his newly minted captain status. Tampa will give them a run for their money!
Rays in 7. Freddy Peralta World Series MVP, because why not. He enters in desperation relief to get the final out.

Jacob Misiorowski is incredible, but meet Rays' Junior Caminero, who is the best in baseball at hitting a 100 MPH fastball originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Looking at the World Series matchup, the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays have a great opportunity to win this.
The Brewers are a great team from top to bottom and don't make many mistakes, while the Rays keep winning with elite starting pitching, timely hitting, and a superstar in Junior Caminero.
Caminero might be one of the better players in Major League Baseball, but unfortunately, outside of fans who truly follow the game, he doesn't get as much hype as he deserves.
As weird as that might sound for a guy who hit 42 home runs this season and 45 last year, it feels like Caminero doesn't get the respect he deserves.
Misiorowski is well known, even to casual fans, because of how hard he throws. He's a guy who's going to consistently throw 100-plus miles per hour.
But here's the thing: Caminero is arguably the best hitter in Major League Baseball on high-velocity pitches. According to BaseballThings.com, he's hitting .358 with a ridiculous .580 OPS on pitches 96-plus miles per hour.
Baseball fans are in for a treat when these two meet, as Misiorowski will toe the rubber in Game 1.
They've gone at it before, and Misiorowski has struck Caminero out twice in three at-bats, with the Rays slugger failing to get a hit. Caminero keeps proving he can step up in big moments, so it wouldn't be surprising to see him get Misiorowski this time around.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski set to make MLB World Series history two pitches into Game 1 originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will meet for what's expected to be a very exciting World Series. In Game 1, we'll get to watch a guy like Jacob Misiorowski toe the rubber and throw at a level we haven't really seen before in this league, at least in the World Series.
Game 1 of the World Series won't make or break the series, but the Brewers and Rays have to feel that if they get off to a good start, they're in a better position than if they don't.
The Rays also have one of their big-time arms ready to go, with right-hander Nick Martinez expected to start Game 1.
It was surprising that Drew Rasmussen didn't get the ball, as Rasmussen is among the best starters in Major League Baseball and has been lights out all year, posting a 2.67 ERA in the regular season.
He's also been lights out in the postseason, posting a one-hit, eight-inning showing against the New York Yankees in the ALDS, plus two starts against the Cleveland Guardians in which he went at least 6.0 innings and allowed only one and two runs, respectively.
But for Misiorowski, there is more for all baseball fans to consider.
We'll get to see somebody make history, as his fastball is going to light up the radar gun. According to the latest, there's only been one pitch thrown by a starter in a World Series game at 101-plus miles per hour since 2008. Misiorowski is bound to change that in a major way.
"Only 1 pitch has been thrown by a starting pitcher in a World Series game at 101+ MPH in the entire pitch tracking era (2008-now).
"That is about to change," Codify Baseball wrote.
There's a very good chance we'll see 101-plus from Misiorowski throughout the game, and he'll probably have a couple of 103-pluses.
This is a guy who has a fastball that we've never seen before from a starting pitcher, and while some Major League Baseball fans might not love that it's two small-market teams going at it, we're going to see a boatload of talent, and he's one of the guys who's going to provide that.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski ridiculously did something 89% of the time with 102+ MPH fastball originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will meet in the World Series, starting Friday night in what's expected to be one of the more exciting World Series we've seen in quite some time.
Based on talent and other factors, both teams are equally matched, with small markets and young superstar talent.
For the Brewers, there might not be a bigger young superstar pitcher in Major League Baseball than Jacob Misiorowski. All Misiorowski has done this year is throw baseball at a ridiculous level, with the expectation that he'll win the National League Cy Young Award.
Misiorowski hasn't been bad by any means in the postseason, but also hasn't been great. He's thrown only 8.1 innings in his first two starts, with at least 88 pitches in each.
He still only allowed one earned run against the Los Angeles Dodgers and two against the San Diego Padres.
Misiorowski arguably has the best fastball in Major League Baseball, with some even thinking he has, or could have, the best in MLB history. As for what he's done this season, he's thrown more pitches at 102+ mph than nearly every other starter in baseball history, which is flat-out ridiculous.
"There have been 412 pitches thrown by MLB starters at 102+ MPH in the entire pitch tracking era and Jacob Misiorowski threw 365 of them this season. It's completely ridiculous," Codify Baseball wrote.
The biggest question Misiorowski will have to answer in the World Series is whether he can stay on the mound for six-plus innings.
Even during parts of the regular season, it wasn't exactly like this was a workhorse throwing complete games left and right. He hasn't thrown more than 6.1 innings in any start since Aug. 2, though multiple factors could explain it, as the Brewers arguably have the best bullpen in Major League Baseball and trust a lot of guys coming in during the back half of games.

item.title: [mlb.com] Our experts make their World Series predictions
item.dc:creator: Max Ralph
item.description: The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. item.content:encoded:
The Brewers, whose 103 regular-season wins were a franchise record, navigated a tight NL Division Series against the Padres before clobbering the two-time reigning champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series sweep. It’s just the second World Series appearance in their history and their first since 1982.
Meanwhile, the Rays swept the division rival Yankees in the ALDS before handling the Guardians in six games in the ALCS. They’re back in the Fall Classic for the third time and the first since 2020.
Both teams do a little bit of everything right on the diamond, making for what should be a thoroughly exciting World Series. Here’s how our group of MLB.com experts see it playing out.
Rays vs. Brewers
The pick: Brewers (43 of 51 votes, 84.3%)
Why they’ll win
Any time you take down the back-to-back reigning champs, and do so in a sweep, it’s going to make noise. But really, this is nothing new for the 2026 Brewers. They owned the best regular-season record with a roster that just gets the job done across the board.
The Brewers can play small ball, but they can slug when it matters most, too. In fact, Milwaukee has been more homer-dependent in October than it was all year. But the club can still work a deep count and get on base in many ways. Just ask Jake Bauers.
On the mound, it’s no secret that the bullpen is the Brewers’ strength. One of the best groups in the regular season is only doing more of the same in October, with a 1.33 ERA in eight games. Lefty Aaron Ashby is leading the charge during a historically good run. And then there’s that Jacob Misiorowski guy, who has been good enough in the playoffs but could unleash a new, dominant level in the World Series.
What they’re saying
“There's something about this Brewers club. Maintaining the league's best record all summer and barely giving an inch so far in the postseason, they're looking pretty unstoppable with the right mix of clutch hits, key performers and an absolutely lockdown bullpen. It might finally be the Crew's moment in the spotlight.” -- Adrian Garro, editorial producer
“The Brewers have been knocking on this door for years and are firing on all cylinders following their impressive sweep of the Dodgers. They are smart and hard-nosed enough not to let the long layoff affect them negatively.” -- Andrew Werle, supervising editor, content operations
“Walking off Mason Miller. Sweeping the 2-time defending champion Dodgers. These Brewers may just be a team of destiny, with their final obstacle being the American League's top-seeded Rays.” -- Kyle Boris, supervisor, media operations
The dissenting view
The Brewers have been dominant, but so have the Rays. They have a clear edge in starting pitching, with Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez firing on all cylinders. The Tampa Bay bullpen, while not as overpowering as the Brewers’, is still strong and has lockdown closer Bryan Baker waiting in the wings.
The key for the Rays likely lies in their lineup, where Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda appear to be heating up at the right time. Much like Milwaukee, the Rays will put together quality at-bats, get on base and then cause havoc on the basepaths. Perhaps no one is more adept at doing so than Chandler Simpson.
“The Rays' ‘small ball’ doesn't slump, and they've been pressing all of the right pitching buttons.” -- Jonathan Mayo, national reporter, prospects
“With their Big 3 of Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero breaking out at the end of the ALCS -- plus a slight edge over the Crew in starting pitching -- I believe the Rays are going to steal Game 1 vs. The Miz and ride that to a World Series title. Third time is a charm.” -- Brian McGrath, supervising editor, content operations
Series predictions
Brewers (6 games): 23 votes
Brewers (7 games): 14 votes
Brewers (5 games): 5 votes
Rays (7 games): 4 votes
Rays (6 games): 3 votes
Rays (5 games): 1 vote
Brewers (4 games): 1 vote
There may have been an overwhelming majority of our group predicting the Brewers to win the World Series, but that doesn’t do justice to how close these two teams seem to be. This will: 44 of 51 voters see the series going at least six games.
Who will be named World Series MVP?
Jackson Chourio (MIL): 16 votes
William Contreras (MIL): 13 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL): 6 votes
Yandy Díaz (TB): 5 votes
Brice Turang (MIL): 5 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL): 1 vote
Jake Bauers (MIL): 1 vote
Junior Caminero (TB): 1 vote
Trevor Megill (MIL): 1 vote
Drew Rasmussen (TB): 1 vote
Chandler Simpson (TB): 1 vote
It’s not hard to see why Chourio was our experts’ favorite to take home the World Series Most Valuable Player Award. Still just 22 years old, Chourio already leads Brewers franchise history with six career playoff home runs. He’s already shown he can rise to the occasion this year with a walk-off single against Mason Miller in the NLDS and a massive homer against Blake Snell in the NLCS. But Chourio’s overall production this October has been quiet (6-for-35). It might just be a matter of time before he breaks out.
“Chourio is due to break out in the World Series. While he hasn't done much in the playoffs so far, his two homers were impactful -- a go-ahead shot and a game-tying blast. He's ready to let it rip.” -- Kelsie Heneghan, senior coordinator, social media editorial, MiLB
“He's a legend in the making. This is the start of his Hall of Fame case.” -- Will Leitch, senior columnist
Who will be on the mound when the series ends … and what happens?
Trevor Megill (MIL), final out: 24 votes
Aaron Ashby (MIL), final out: 10 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), final out: 6 votes
Jacob Misiorowski (MIL), final out: 6 votes
Bryan Baker (TB), walked off: 3 votes
Drew Rasmussen (TB), final out: 1 vote
Ian Seymour (TB), final out: 1 vote
Megill has been lights-out as the Brewers’ closer, so it’s easy to envision him shutting things down at American Family Field in Game 6 or 7. But don’t be surprised if it’s Ashby continuing his fireman role -- or The Miz coming in for a clutch relief appearance.

item.title: [prpeak.com] World Series preview: Surprising Brewers-Rays matchup will open with Jacob Misiorowski's record heat

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — The Miz will try to whiz his famous fastball by batters on baseball's biggest stage, opening a new-look World Series between teams guaranteed to produce a first-time champion.
Jacob Misiorowski brings his record-setting heat to the mound for the Milwaukee Brewers on Friday night when he throws the first pitch of the best-of-seven championship against the Tampa Bay Rays, a matchup of modest-money marvels who bumped off glamorous rivals with a throwback base-to-base style.
“Forrest Gump, everyone,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Thursday, introducing his ace to the assembled media.
“I'm still fresh to all of this and I have no idea what the hell is going on,” Misiorowski said a few minutes later.
Few predicted this pairing of pennant winners when the season opened March 25. The first World Series with robot umpires is the first since 1980 between teams seeking their first championship and also could be the first with a 104 mph pitch — thanks to Misiorowski — and the first to be played totally indoors.
Milwaukee is in the Series for the second time after a 44-year absence — an appropriate number given that it was the jersey of the Cream City's most famous baseball player, Hank Aaron, who became a star with the Milwaukee Braves in the 1950s and ended his career with the expansion Brewers in the 1970s.
Both teams fell short in previous Series trips, the Brewers losing to St. Louis in 1982 and the Rays to Philadelphia in 2008 and to the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2020. Not since the Phillies beat Kansas City in 1980 have two teams met seeking their first title. The time before that was in 1920.
Rays players are excited to display their brand of baseball.
“We love watching those guys cause chaos,” Tampa Bay pitcher Steven Matz said of his team's bunters and speedsters. “Every time it’s first and third and someone lays down a bunt, we are just dying laughing in the bullpen.”
Misiorowski is likely to set a World Series velocity record
Misiorowski, a 24-year-old right-hander in his first full major league season, is a starting pitcher like no other. He threw 1,115 pitches of 100 mph or higher this year — shattering the old high of 673 since tracking began in 2008, by Jordan Hicks in 2018.
His fastest pitch was 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27, and he appears likely to break the 101.1 mph record for a Series starter by the New York Mets' Noah Syndergaard in 2015 and possibly the overall Series high of 103.2 mph by Cubs reliever Aroldis Chapman to Cleveland's Coco Crisp in Game 2 of 2016.
Misiorowski didn't finish the fifth inning in either of his first two postseason starts this year. Batters have swung at 94 of his 182 postseason pitches and fouled off 51 — 28% of pitches and 54% of swings.
“He hasn’t been as crisp,” Murphy said. “They’re obviously looking at an area. They’re trying to exploit everything. He’s exposed, like all these guys get at some point.”
Martinez a surprise starter for Rays
Nick Martinez will start for Tampa Bay, which gives extra rest to Drew Rasmussen ahead of Game 2 and Freddy Peralta before Game 3.
A 36-year-old right-hander with his fourth major league team, Martinez took the Rays to dinner Wednesday at Carnevor, a top Milwaukee steakhouse. He invites teammates, who have nicknamed him “El Presidente,” to a restaurant in every road city.
“To when I first got to the league, I’ve been around guys that knew how to control a clubhouse and for lack of a better term, knew how to throw a party,” Martinez said. “Getting the guys together is important. Creating that off-the-field chemistry translates to on the field.”
Brewers and Rays have throwback offenses
In an age where power bats usually rule, Milwaukee scored a major league-low 32.1% of its runs on homers and Tampa Bay was second-lowest at 34.4%, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
Brewers captain Christian Yelich says “we’ve done a good job of being kind of chameleons.”
“It's cool that you don't have to be the team to hit 170 home runs a game or whatever,” Misiorowski said. “You can win a baseball game so many different ways.”
Rays batters had the fewest strikeouts among the 30 teams and Tampa Bay’s 45 sacrifice bunts were the most among American League teams since 2015.
“If we had a club that was built with a bunch of boppers, we probably wouldn’t be bunting and stealing bases,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I think we already have made bunting cool.”
After back-to-back Dodgers titles, MLB will have a small-payroll champion
This marks the first time since 1991 that both Series teams are in the bottom half of payrolls: the Brewers were 19th as of Aug. 31 and the Rays 25th. Milwaukee, MLB's smallest market, could become the first small-market champion since Kansas City in 2015. The Rays rank 15th in market size.
To reach the Series, the Brewers swept the deep-pocketed, two-time champion Dodgers in the NL Championship Series and the Rays swept the New York Yankees in an AL Division Series.
Yelich, the highest-paid player in the Series, was 44th overall in the majors on opening day. Yandy Díaz, who earns most among the Rays, ranked 154th.
Robot umps are changing games
Batters have succeeded on 63% of challenges during the postseason in the first year of the Automated Ball-Strike System, winning 40 of 63 appeals to the robot umps. That is up from 49% during the regular season.
Catchers' 58% success rate in the playoffs (58 of 99) is down a tick from 59% during the regular season and pitchers are 1 for 1 — Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax made the only challenge. The 60% overall rate is up from 54% in the regular season.
Tampa Bay's batters have yet to make a postseason challenge. Milwaukee's have won 4 of 7, including a perfect 2 for 2 by Jake Bauers.
Brewers catcher William Contreras has won 60% (12 of 20) and Rays catcher Liam Hicks 67% (8 of 12).
Rest vs. rust: Extra time off hasn't been helpful in recent years
Milwaukee will have had seven days off going into the opener.
While teams with less rest are 15-15 in the Series since Wild Card Era started in 1995, they are 12-4 since 2009.
___
Ronald Blum, The Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Oct 2026, 04:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Benny Sieu)
MILWAUKEE -- The Milwaukee Brewers will be looking for hard-throwing Jacob Misiorowski to regain his dominant regular-season form against the visiting Tampa Bay Rays on Friday in the opening game of the World Series.
Misiorowski, who often tops 100 mph with his fastball, will be opposed by veteran right-hander Nick Martinez in a matchup of teams that have not won the World Series. It is the first meeting of two teams without a World Series title since the Philadelphia Phillies topped the Kansas City Royals in six games in 1980.
Milwaukee, which won a franchise-record 103 games during the regular season, advanced with a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, while the Rays ousted the Cleveland Guardians in six games in the American League Championship Series.
The Brewers' only other World Series appearance was in 1982 when they were in the American League. The charismatic 'Harvey's Wallbangers' lost 6-3 to the St. Louis Cardinals in the decisive seventh game.
The Rays will be making their third World Series appearance. They lost to Philadelphia in five games in 2008 and in six games to the Dodgers in 2020.
Misiorowski, considered the favorite for the NL Cy Young Award, was 16-5 with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. The latter two stats were best in the majors.
But the 24-year-old right-hander did not make it through five innings in either postseason start, although the Brewers rallied to win both games. They topped the San Diego Padres 3-2 in Game 1 of the National League Division Series and the Dodgers 2-1 in the NLCS opener.
'I feel good. I feel like the first one might have been a little under what I expected, but the second one was pretty much right where I wanted to be,' Misiorowski said.
Misiorowski worked out of trouble in his postseason starts, allowing three runs on nine hits in 8 1/3 innings with 11 strikeouts and four walks.
'He hasn't been as crisp,' Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. 'I don't think people are up there thinking it's going to be 104 (mph), and I think they're elated if it's anything less than that. They're obviously looking at an area. They're trying to exploit everything. He's exposed, like all these guys get at some point.'
At the back end, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed six runs over 40 2/3 innings for a 1.33 ERA in the postseason. Closer Trevor Megill has four saves after collecting 30 in the regular season.
Milwaukee was last in the NL in home runs (154) during the regular season but leads all teams in the postseason with 10 homers in eight games. The Rays have hit seven in nine games.
Catcher William Contreras batted .367 with three homers and five RBIs over the Brewers' first two series. Outfielder Jackson Chourio hit .171, but he had two homers and a team-high seven RBIs.
Jake Bauers, who reached the majors with the Rays in 2018, was named the NLCS Most Valuable Player after hitting .286 with one homer and six RBIs against the Dodgers. Bauers set career highs with 26 homers and 86 RBIs during the regular season.
The 36-year-old Martinez pitched in the postseason with San Diego in 2022 and the Cincinnati Reds last season, but he will be making his World Series debut Friday. Ace Drew Rasmussen will start Game 2 with an extra day's rest, with former Brewers ace Freddy Peralta to follow in Game 3.
'It's exciting,' Martinez said Thursday. 'I think as a team, as a staff, we're confident in whoever we call up for the mound. It fell on me, and my job is just to rack up as many outs as we can and keep us in this ballgame.'
Martinez picked up the win in Game 4 of the ALCS when the Rays evened the series with a 7-3 victory at Cleveland. He allowed one run on two hits in 5 1/3 innings.
'He was pitching in pretty cold weather in Cleveland,' said Rays manager Kevin Cash, who was also at the helm for the 2020 World Series. 'Made some adjustments, he got the strike throwing where he wanted, the cutter gone, and the changeup. I don't even know, somebody told me he changed his grip in between innings, between the first and second. I'm glad I didn't know that in the moment.'
Martinez also started Game 3 in the Rays' ALDS sweep of the New York Yankees. He gave up two runs in 3 2/3 innings in an eventual 4-3 Tampa Bay victory.
Martinez is 0-1 with a 4.44 ERA in 12 regular-season games (seven starts) against Milwaukee. He has a 2.93 ERA in eight games at American Family Field.
Rays closer Bryan Baker, who tied for the MLB lead with 41 saves, has five saves in five postseason chances, pitching in seven of the nine games.
Third baseman Junior Caminero, whose 42 homers were second in the AL, has just one hit in 33 at-bats in the postseason.
--Jim Hoehn, Field Level Media

item.title: [mlb.com] Rays-Brewers World Series position-by-position breakdown

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

item.content:encoded:
The 2025 season provided ideal outcomes for fantasy managers who invested in elite starting pitchers. That season, Tarik Skubal, Paul Skenes, Garrett Crochet and Zack Wheeler were the top four pitchers drafted. Per our Fantasy Player Rater, Skubal ($35.5), Crochet ($32.8) and Skenes ($30.8) finished 1-2-3 among starting pitchers in all roto formats. Wheeler finished 14th ($22.6) despite his season being cut short. As is the case every single year, to varying degrees, there were mid-round arms who produced elite roto seasons (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Max Fried), as well starters such as Nathan Eovaldi, Matthew Boyd, and Trevor Rogers who provided hefty profit a as late-round picks and free agent acquisitions.
As is also the case every season, there were early-round landmines. Cole Ragans, Blake Snell, and Corbin Burnes all missed at least two-thirds of the season due to injuries. Logan Gilbert investors certainly weren’t thrilled about his abbreviated season with only six wins. Nevertheless, dream seasons from the Crème de la crème instilled an illusion of tranquility at the top of the SP pool for 2026 drafts despite the position’s inherent risks and volatile history.
The calm ominously turned to storm on Opening Day. Paul Skenes couldn’t get out of the first inning against the Mets, allowing five earned runs, as droves of social media melodramatics scolded us: “…and that’s why you never draft pitchers early!” Skenes (174 IP – 200 K – 10 W – 3.82 – 1.12) inevitably lost “fantasy god” status as his price dropped a couple of rounds for 2027 drafts. Skubal was a top 10 pitcher with elite ratios, but did not have his usual season of dominance due to missing 5-6 starts. Crochet was an injury landmine and one of many early-round busts.
There were some wins in the second tier (Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale) as well as disappointments (Bryan Woo, Hunter Brown, Ragans again), but what may be most memorable about last season’s starting pitcher pool was that leagues were won without having to invest in early starting pitchers at all. Of course, that only happened to managers who side-stepped the early-round hitter landmines like Aaron Judge, Ronald Acuña Jr., Vladimir Guerrero Jr., Francisco Lindor and Cal Raleigh. The two top producers – Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler – were post-100 ADP picks. Of the 19 starters who earned $14 or more in 12-team leagues, 13 had an ADP of 100+, including six with an ADP of 250 or greater.
| # | Player | Team | ADP | Min Pick | Max Pick | SP Rank | $ Earned |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2 | Cam Schlittler | NYY | 119.2 | 85 | 173 | 2 | $37.1 |
| 3 | Yoshinobu Yamamoto | LAD | 26.5 | 10 | 41 | 3 | $30.6 |
| 4 | Chris Sale | ATL | 39.1 | 24 | 54 | 4 | $28.5 |
| 5 | Drew Rasmussen | TB | 137.4 | 62 | 176 | 5 | $28.4 |
| 6 | Dylan Cease | TOR | 76.0 | 38 | 98 | 6 | $23.5 |
| 7 | Jesús Luzardo | PHI | 71.5 | 44 | 95 | 7 | $22.9 |
| 8 | Tarik Skubal | DET | 6.9 | 3 | 12 | 8 | $22.8 |
| 9 | Parker Messick | CLE | 287.6 | 183 | 355 | 9 | $22.1 |
| 10 | Cristopher Sánchez | PHI | 25.3 | 3 | 36 | 10 | $21.8 |
| 11 | Zack Wheeler | PHI | 112.8 | 71 | 153 | 11 | $20.8 |
| 12 | Sonny Gray | BOS | 138.1 | 87 | 182 | 12 | $20.1 |
| 13 | Chase Burns | CIN | 107.0 | 80 | 176 | 13 | $18.1 |
| 14 | Logan Henderson | MLW | 295.7 | 221 | 360 | 14 | $17.6 |
| 15 | Gavin Williams | CLE | 144.3 | 81 | 223 | 15 | $16.9 |
| 16 | Cade Cavalli | WAS | 305.4 | 243 | 360 | 16 | $16.6 |
| 17 | Nick Martinez | TB | 359.7 | 291 | 359 | 17 | $14.3 |
| 18 | Reid Detmers | LAA | 318.7 | 237 | 357 | 18 | $14.2 |
| 19 | Braxton Ashcraft | PIT | 246.6 | 193 | 317 | 19 | $14.0 |
SP Rank and $ Earned from the FanGraphs Fantasy Player Rater (12-team)
A quick review of this group shouldn’t elicit much bewilderment besides maybe Nick Martinez. Most of the other top performers with a post-100 ADP were former prospects with breakout and profit potential. Let’s run through each set of five rounds by 2026 NFBC Online Championship (OC) 12-team ADP to review results in relation to draft price. Expect some takeaways for 2027 drafts along the way. Pitchers who were traded are listed with the team they were on in March.
| Player | Team | ADP | SP Rank | $ Earned |
|---|---|---|---|---|

These are the pitchers with ADPs in the first five rounds of OCs. Ohtani could technically be excluded since he was mostly used as a hitter in NFBC formats last season. He did earn nearly $14, producing sparkling ratios (1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP) with 95 strikeouts in 85.2 innings (14 starts). Ohtani should pitch again next season, but will be a top-three consensus fantasy pick regardless. No matter where he signs, Skubal will be the first or second SP off draft boards, along with Misiorowski. Sale, Yamamoto and Cristopher Sánchez will likely live in the Round 2 range. Sale was the SP3 in 2024, SP20 in 2025 and SP4 in 2026. Yamamoto was the SP7 and SP3 in his first two full Major League seasons. Sánchez has posted consecutive seasons of 200+ innings and a sub-3.00 ERA. Hunter Brown will be a polarizing pick in the Rounds 4-7 range coming off a 20-start season where he produced a strong 3.19 ERA, but saw his WHIP and walk rate balloon from the previous season — from 1.03 and 7.8% to 1.27 and 12.2%.
A fantasy bust in 2026, Freddy Peralta is quickly surging back up confidence meters and draft boards with his dominant playoff performances. Bryan Woo and Logan Gilbert will be slightly discounted coming off disappointing seasons, but T-Mobile Park in Seattle remains advantageous to starting pitchers (30-of-30 in MLB Park Factor for hits in 2026) and bounce-backs wouldn’t be shocking, assuming good health. Ragans underwent UCL repair surgery in July and has a 10-12 month return timetable, so he’s off our radars for the forseeable future. Jacob deGrom was slightly more human in his age-38 season, posting a career-worst 4.20 ERA, albeit with a 3.11 FIP, 3.14 xFIP and 3.15 SIERA.
Fried’s UCL is “in a good place” according to NY Daily News writer, Gary Phillips. Logan Webb is no longer the position’s Iron Man and could fall out of the top 100 ADP, though he will always have supporters. A healthy Webb could provide profit at a reasonable cost.

The 61-120 ADP range was quite the mixed bag.
Dylan Cease and Jesús Luzardo were studs and will be drafted in the top 50 in most formats.
Wheeler recovered thoroughly from his thoracic outlet procedure and produced yet another $20+ season: 162 IP (28 starts) – 193 K – 14 W – 3.00 – 1.05. He has been the best pitcher in the Majors since 2021, leading in wins (79), ERA (2.92) and second in strikeouts (1,234) behind Cease’s 1,345.
Chase Burns will be highly coveted after his masterful performance over his first full season (154.1 IP – 185 K – 15 W – 2.86 – 1.17) and will be drafted among the top 12 to 15 starters. Nolan McLean will be slightly cheaper than Burns after his first full and successful season in the Majors. Cases made against either this offseason will start with concerns about their lack of elite control and potential WHIP damage at Tier 2 SP prices. Eury Pérez is in this boat as well after posting a 10.3% walk rate and a 1.21 WHIP, though don’t expect to pay anything but a premium for the coveted fireballer who will turn 24 in April.
Joe Ryan should be a solid pick among the top 100 as well. Though he may never have that 180+ IP dream season where good health and all the cards align, Ryan has been a dependable fantasy stud, posting a K-BB% over 20% for four straight seasons and has made between 23 and 30 starts over his first five full seasons.
There were quite a few negative value guys in this range, which was quite shocking for some: George Kirby, Kyle Bradish, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman and Emmet Sheehan. Kirby is quickly becoming persona non grata in the fantasy community, posting a painful 1.40 WHIP last season and two straight years with a 4.00+ ERA. Bradish’s WHIP (1.42) was even worse than Kirby’s as he did most of his damage after the All-Star break, posting a 5.29 ERA and a .398 wOBA in those final 10 starts before getting shelved due to lower abdominal pain and being diagnosed with a sports hernia. Gausman compiled 30+ starts for a sixth consecutive season. Despite nearly all of his rate stats and underlying metrics matching last season’s, Gausman posted a 4.51 ERA, with an xFIP and SIERA over a full run lower. I’ll remind myself of how solid everything looked under the hood for Gausman and would consider targeting him again in 2027 drafts. Sheehan isn’t going to fly under the radar this draft season despite last year’s poor results. The key here, of course, is Sheehan having a rotation spot. He dominated in his time down in Triple-A and fired three gems for the Dodgers in September (0.53 ERA, 24:3 K:BB in 17 innings/3 starts).
