item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will play a Suds vs. Sun World Series that will produce a first-time champion and likely baseball's first all-indoor championship.
The best-of-seven showdown between low-payroll pennant winners opens Friday night in Milwaukee. It'll be the first World Series between title-less teams since the Philadelphia Phillies defeated the Kansas City Royals in 1980 and just the second since 1910.
One city is known for the television sitcom “ Laverne & Shirley," the home of Harley-Davidson motorcycles, cheeseheads and breweries that have included Miller, Pabst and Schlitz. The other is a vacation destination featuring warm weather, beaches and art museums.
“They’re highly athletic but so are we. I’m excited to see two great teams that play the game a little differently than maybe it’s been played the last decade or so,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after his team defeated Cleveland in six games for the AL pennant. “We’re going to use our speed. We’re going to bunt when it’s called for. We’ll try to get matchups and I can assure you they’re going to do the same.”
Just five of the current 30 teams have never won a title, with Colorado, San Diego and Seattle also ringless.
“The city is ready. I know that the fans are ready, and I know that we’ll be ready,” said Milwaukee's Jake Bauers, MVP of the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NL Championship Series.
Milwaukee's Jacob Misiorowski heads the pitchers with his 100 mph-plus heat, and each team features a dynamic 22-year-old anchoring the lineup: Jackson Chourio of the Brewers and Junior Caminero of the Rays. Tampa Bay's Freddy Peralta and Drew Rasmussen could pitch against their former team.
“I don’t know how the people, the fans are going to take it, but I’m happy to be go there,” said Peralta, the ALCS MVP. “I have a lot of people that I love over there, people that care about me and I’m happy to be there and be able to compete together and take a lot of pictures and videos."
The Brewers started as the expansion Seattle Pilots in 1969, then were bought by Bud Selig's group in bankruptcy court and moved to Milwaukee for the 1970 season. The team's only Series trip was a seven-game loss to St. Louis in the 1982 Suds Series, back when the Brewers were in the American League.
Tampa Bay launched as the expansion Devil Rays in 1998 and dropped the “Devil” ahead of the 2008 season. The team's two Series appearances ended with losses to Philadelphia in 2008 and the Dodgers in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season.
Best face each other for 6th time in wild-card era
This will be only the sixth time since the start of the wild-card era in 1995 that teams with the top records in each league meet in the World Series after Atlanta-Cleveland (1995), New York Yankees-Braves (1999), Boston-St. Louis (2013), Dodgers-Rays (2020) and Dodgers-Yankees (2024).
Two low-payroll teams in Series for first time in 35 years
Milwaukee had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31. Tampa Bay was 25th.
Not since 1991 had both pennant winners been among the bottom 50% in player spending. Minnesota was 15th among 26 teams when it beat Atlanta (19th) in seven games.
Matchup with a ceiling
Tampa Bay’s ballpark has a fixed roof and Milwaukee’s is retractable — it probably will be closed with game-time temperatures predicted to be in the upper 40s or low 50s.
When all World Series games were played at retractable-roof ballparks in 2020 (Texas) and 2023 (Texas and Arizona), there were three open-air games each year.
The roofs of both ballparks came into play this postseason.
In the ninth inning of Milwaukee’s 3-2 win over the Padres in Game 1 of their NL Division Series, San Diego’s Ty France hit a high drive that appeared it might be headed over the left-field wall for a go-ahead homer until it struck a cable on the retractable roof in Milwaukee.
Two nights later, Yankees rookie Spencer Jones hit a flyball off a catwalk at Tropicana Field that was caught by Rays right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. for an out in the second inning of New York’s 5-2 loss in Game 2 of their AL Division Series.
Common ties
Greg Vaughn, Willy Adames and Matt Garza are the most prominent players with lengthy stretches on both teams, and Bauers made his big league debut with the Rays in 2018.
Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked for the Rays for nine years before Milwaukee hired him as an assistant GM in October 2015.
One of baseball's great nicknames
Those 1982 Brewers were known as Harvey's Wallbangers, a nickname given by first baseman Cecil Cooper. The Brewers led the major leagues in home runs under manager Harvey Kuenn and had a roster with five future Hall of Famers: Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Rollie Fingers, Ted Simmons and Don Sutton.
Haunted hotel?
Various players over the years have claimed The Pfister Hotel, where many teams stay in Milwaukee, is haunted. Opened in 1893, the hotel has Romanesque Revival architecture, and players have claimed to hear spooky noises and footsteps.
If there is a Game 7, it would be played in Milwaukee on Halloween night.
Boss Man
Milwaukee's Pat Murphy, winner of the last two NL Manager of the Year awards, has two tattoos referencing Bruce Springsteen: “No Retreat No Surrender” on his left forearm and “The Boss” on his back.
He first went to a Springsteen concert in 1980 when he was in college, then another when he was coaching at Notre Dame.
“He grew up a Catholic kid in New Jersey. I was a Catholic kid from upstate New York,” the 67-year-old Murphy said. “There’s just so much that resonates with me how he speaks about things.”
Ballpark histories
The 1982 Series was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, home of the Braves from 1953-65 before they moved to Atlanta, and then the Brewers from 1970-2000. This year's championship will be played at American Family Field. Known as Miller Park from 2001-20, the ballpark is adjacent to the County Stadium site. It was host of the 2002 All-Star Game, which ended in a 7-7, 11-inning tie after both teams ran out of pitchers.
Milwaukee's ballpark is known for its Racing Sausages in the middle of the sixth inning, with the Brat, Polish, Italian, Hot Dog and Chorizo competing. It also has the Uecker Seat in the last row of section 422 in the left-field upper deck — it includes a bronze statue of Bob Uecker, the beloved funny man who broadcast Brewers games for 54 seasons until his death last year.
Tampa Bay's home, Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, is on its third name. Known as the Florida Suncoast Dome from 1990-93 and the ThunderDome from 1993-96, the stadium got its current name about 18 months before the Rays' first game in 1998.
Its only prior World Series games were in 2008, when the Rays split the first two games against Philadelphia before the Phillies won three straight at home. Tampa Bay's other Series appearance was in 2020, when due to the coronavirus pandemic the entire series was played at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas.
The Trop reopened this season after repairs to damage caused by Hurricane Milton. The Rays plan to move to a new stadium across the bay in Tampa in 2029.
Jersey watch
Milwaukee went 29-13 in cream uniforms during the regular season, 17-7 in pinstripes, 27-12 in navy blue, 9-6 in City Connect outfits and 21-21 in light blue. During the postseason, the Brewers are 4-0 in cream and 3-1 in navy.
Tampa Bay was 36-19 in home white, 32-33 in road navy, 8-2 in road Columbia blue, 12-3 in Devil Rays throwback jerseys, 6-4 in City Connect and 3-3 in road gray. In the playoffs, the Rays are 2-1 in home white, 2-0 in Devil Rays throwbacks and 3-1 in road gray.

Milwaukee was 32 for 128 (.250) and had a .347 on-base percentage in its NLCS sweep of the Dodgers, the exact same numbers Los Angeles batters had in their NLCS sweep of the Brewers last year.

item.title: [fansided.com] How many teams have never won a World Series? Either Rays or Brewers will make history
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: For the third time in franchise history, the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series. Thanks to another brilliant outing from Freddy Peralta and more big hits from their big three, the Rays polished off the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night. Junior Caminero and the Rays will now take on Jacob Misiorowski, Brice Turang and the NL-winning Milwaukee Brewers in the Fall Classic. Led by ex-Rays prospect and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, the Brewers swept the Dodgers en route to
item.content:encoded:
For the third time in franchise history, the Tampa Bay Rays are headed to the World Series. Thanks to another brilliant outing from Freddy Peralta and more big hits from their big three, the Rays polished off the Cleveland Guardians in Game 6 of the ALCS on Monday night.
Junior Caminero and the Rays will now take on Jacob Misiorowski, Brice Turang and the NL-winning Milwaukee Brewers in the Fall Classic. Led by ex-Rays prospect and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, the Brewers swept the Dodgers en route to capturing their first pennant since 1982.
As if that weren't intriguing enough, we’re guaranteed to see baseball history, as neither the Rays nor the Brewers have won the World Series — and they’re not alone.
Which teams have never won the World Series?
As of October 2026, the Rays and Brewers are among five teams that have never won the World Series:
| Team | World Series appearances |
|---|---|
| Colorado Rockies | 2007 |
| Milwaukee Brewers | 1982, 2026 |
| San Diego Padres | 1984, 1998 |
| Seattle Mariners | N/A |
| Tampa Bay Rays | 2008, 2020, 2026 |
Unsurprisingly, all five franchises are expansion teams, with the Brewers (then the Seattle Pilots) and Padres debuting in 1969. The Mariners followed in 1977, and the Rockies (1993) and Rays (1998) joined in the two most recent expansions.
Who would have guessed the Rays, a franchise that didn’t have a winning record in its first 10 seasons of existence, would own three pennants since the start of 2008? Oh, and they’ve reached the World Series more times in that span than the Yankees, Blue Jays and Orioles. (That sound you hear is Yankees fans removing the chainsaws from their Halloween decorations and finding a new target to scare.)
As we discussed last week, the Brewers could become the second team to win the World Series after switching leagues. The Astros, who spent nearly five decades in the NL, achieved the feat in 2017 and 2022.
Milwaukee’s NLCS victory also means that all 15 National League teams have won a pennant while in the NL.
How did the Brewers and Rays do in their previous World Series appearances?
Well, they lost.
Jokes aside, we’ll head down Memory Lane and start with the 1982 Brewers. Led by Robin Yount and Pete Vuckovich, who respectively won the AL’s MVP and Cy Young Awards, the Brew Crew defeated the then-California Angels in the ALCS to capture their first pennant.
Milwaukee looked destined for a championship parade when the Brewers took a 3-2 World Series lead over the Cardinals. But the shift to St. Louis helped World Series MVP Darrell Porter and the Redbirds bring home their first title since 1967.
Yount was one of five future Hall of Famers on that Brewers team, joining Paul Molitor, Ted Simmons, Don Sutton and Rollie Fingers.
As for the Rays, there’s not much to say about their first World Series appearance. Chase Utley and the Phillies handled them with relative ease in 2008, and the greatest issue that October was the weather. If you’ve never experienced late-October rain in the Northeast, consider yourselves lucky.
The 2020 World Series was both forgettable and immensely more memorable, which is quite the contradiction. But the less said about 2020 as a whole, the better. Randy Arozarena’s postseason breakout is really the only thing that we personally remember.
Sorry, Rays fans. For your sake, we hope this year’s Fall Classic isn’t lost to time, too.
Evaluating the Rockies, Padres, and Mariners’ 2027 World Series chances
Forget whatever the way-too-early odds or prediction markets tell you … except as it relates to the Rockies’ World Series chances. You can effectively pencil them in for yet another losing record in 2027, regardless of how many games they play amid a potentially shortened season.
As we’ve discussed, speculation is growing that the Padres will make significant roster changes — including potentially trading likely future Hall of Fame third baseman Manny Machado — following an ownership change. Superstar outfielder/second baseman Fernando Tatis Jr. is likely safe, as is veteran shortstop Xander Bogaerts.
The Padres’ new ownership group recently emailed fans, saying the team is “all-in” ahead of the 2027 season. What that means, and whether it matters, depends on whether you’re an optimist or a pessimist.
We mentioned Arozarena earlier, and he’s a pending free agent who isn’t expected to re-sign with the Mariners. Seattle still hasn’t replaced Dan Wilson, and the organization overall reeks of dysfunction. If that sounds harsh, look no further than Cal Raleigh’s lack of leadership and the Mariners forcing Wilson to announce his own firing.
That said, the Padres have the best chance of these three to reach the 2027 World Series, though that’s not saying much.

item.title: [fox11online.com] Brewers-Rays will produce a first-time champion
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM AP Baseball Writer
item.description: Brewers-Rays will produce a first-time champion The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will play a Suds vs. Sun World Series that will produce a first-time champion and likely baseball's first all-indoor championship. The best-of-seven showdown between low-payroll pennant winners opens Friday night in Milwaukee. It'll be the first World Series between title-less teams since the Philadelphia Phillies defeated the Kansas City Royals in 1980. One city is known for the television sitcom “ Laverne
item.content:encoded:
Brewers-Rays will produce a first-time champion
The Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays will play a Suds vs. Sun World Series that will produce a first-time champion and likely baseball's first all-indoor championship.
The best-of-seven showdown between low-payroll pennant winners opens Friday night in Milwaukee. It'll be the first World Series between title-less teams since the Philadelphia Phillies defeated the Kansas City Royals in 1980.
One city is known for the television sitcom “ Laverne & Shirley," the home of Harley-Davidson motorcycles, cheeseheads and breweries that have included Miller, Pabst and Schlitz. The other is a vacation destination featuring warm weather, beaches and art museums.
Just five of the current 30 teams have never won a title, with Colorado, San Diego and Seattle also ringless.
“The city is ready. I know that the fans are ready, and I know that we’ll be ready,” said Milwaukee's Jake Bauers, MVP of the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NL Championship Series.
Milwaukee's Jacob Misiorowski heads the pitchers with his 100 mph-plus heat, and each team features a dynamic 22-year-old anchoring the lineup: Jackson Chourio of the Brewers and Junior Caminero of the Rays. Tampa Bay's Freddy Peralta and Drew Rasmussen could pitch against their former teams.
The Brewers started as the expansion Seattle Pilots in 1969, then were bought by Bud Selig's group in bankruptcy court and moved to Milwaukee for the 1970 season. The team's only Series trip was a seven-game loss to St. Louis in the 1982 Suds Series, back when the Brewers were in the American League.
Tampa Bay, which defeated Cleveland in six games for the AL pennant, launched as the expansion Devil Rays in 1998 and dropped the “Devil” ahead of the 2008 season. The team's two Series appearances ended with losses to Philadelphia in 2008 and the Dodgers in the pandemic-shortened 2020 season.
Best face each other for 6th time in wild-card era
This will be only the sixth time since the start of the wild-card era in 1995 that teams with the top records in each league meet in the World Series after Atlanta-Cleveland (1995), New York Yankees-Braves (1999), Boston-St. Louis (2013), Dodgers-Rays (2020) and Dodgers-Yankees (2024).
Two low-payroll teams in Series for first time in 35 years
Milwaukee had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31. Tampa Bay was 25th.
Not since 1991 had both pennant winners been among the bottom 50% in player spending. Minnesota was 15th among 26 teams when it beat Atlanta (19th) in seven games.
Matchup with a ceiling
Tampa Bay’s ballpark has a fixed roof and Milwaukee’s is retractable — it probably will be closed with game-time temperatures predicted to be in the upper 40s or low 50s.
When all World Series games were played at retractable-roof ballparks in 2020 (Texas) and 2023 (Texas and Arizona), there were three open-air games each year.
The roofs of both ballparks came into play this postseason.
In the ninth inning of Milwaukee’s 3-2 win over the Padres in Game 1 of their NL Division Series, San Diego’s Ty France hit a high drive that appeared it might be headed over the left-field wall for a go-ahead homer until it struck a cable on the retractable roof in Milwaukee.
Two nights later, Yankees rookie Spencer Jones hit a flyball off a catwalk at Tropicana Field that was caught by Rays right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. for an out in the second inning of New York’s 5-2 loss in Game 2 of their AL Division Series.
Common ties
Greg Vaughn, Willy Adames and Matt Garza are the most prominent players with lengthy stretches on both teams, and Bauers made his big league debut with the Rays in 2018.
Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked for the Rays for nine years before Milwaukee hired him as an assistant GM in October 2015.
One of baseball's great nicknames
Those 1982 Brewers were known as Harvey's Wallbangers, a nickname given by first baseman Cecil Cooper. The Brewers led the major leagues in home runs under manager Harvey Kuenn and had a roster with five future Hall of Famers: Robin Yount, Paul Molitor, Rollie Fingers, Ted Simmons and Don Sutton.
Haunted hotel?
Various players over the years have claimed The Pfister Hotel, where many teams stay in Milwaukee, is haunted. Opened in 1893, the hotel has Romanesque Revival architecture, and players have claimed to hear spooky noises and footsteps.
If there is a Game 7, it would be played in Milwaukee on Halloween night.
Boss Man
Milwaukee's Pat Murphy, winner of the last two NL Manager of the Year awards, has two tattoos referencing Bruce Springsteen: “No Retreat No Surrender” on his left forearm and “The Boss” on his back.
He first went to a Springsteen concert in 1980 when he was in college, then another when he was coaching at Notre Dame.
“He grew up a Catholic kid in New Jersey. I was a Catholic kid from upstate New York,” the 67-year-old Murphy said. “There’s just so much that resonates with me how he speaks about things.”
Ballpark histories
The 1982 Series was played at Milwaukee County Stadium, home of the Braves from 1953-65 before they moved to Atlanta, and then the Brewers from 1970-2000. This year's championship will be played at American Family Field. Known as Miller Park from 2001-20, the ballpark is adjacent to the County Stadium site. It was host of the 2002 All-Star Game, which ended in a 7-7, 11-inning tie after both teams ran out of pitchers.
Milwaukee's ballpark is known for its Racing Sausages in the middle of the sixth inning, with the Brat, Polish, Italian, Hot Dog and Chorizo competing. It also has the Uecker Seat in the last row of section 422 in the left-field upper deck — it includes a bronze statue of Bob Uecker, the beloved funny man who broadcast Brewers games for 54 seasons until his death last year.
Tampa Bay's home, Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, is on its third name. Known as the Florida Suncoast Dome from 1990-93 and the ThunderDome from 1993-96, the stadium got its current name about 18 months before the Rays' first game in 1998.
Its only prior World Series games were in 2008, when the Rays split the first two games against Philadelphia before the Phillies won three straight at home. Tampa Bay's other Series appearance was in 2020, when due to the coronavirus pandemic the entire series was played at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas.
The Trop reopened this season after repairs to damage caused by Hurricane Milton. The Rays plan to move to a new stadium across the bay in Tampa in 2029.
Jersey watch
Milwaukee went 29-13 in cream uniforms during the regular season, 17-7 in pinstripes, 27-12 in navy blue, 9-6 in City Connect outfits and 21-21 in light blue. During the postseason, the Brewers are 4-0 in cream and 3-1 in navy.
Tampa Bay was 36-19 in home white, 32-33 in road navy, 8-2 in road Columbia blue, 12-3 in Devil Rays throwback jerseys, 6-4 in City Connect and 3-3 in road gray. In the playoffs, the Rays are 3-1 in home white, 1-0 in Devil Rays throwbacks and 3-1 in road gray.

item.title: [fansided.com] Rays and Brewers set for World Series showdown in updated MLB playoff bracket
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers
item.description: Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history. Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise histo
item.content:encoded:
Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history.
Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise history. Let's dive in.
Updated MLB playoff bracket after Rays advance to the World Series
And then there were two. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the World Series seemingly eons ago, dispatching of the Los Angeles Dodgers in a shocking sweep. Now that the Rays have knocked off the Guardians in the ALCS, our World Series matchup is set.
- World Series: Tampa Bay Rays (AL champs) vs. Milwaukee Brewers (NL champs)
It's not all that often that the top seed in each league meets in the Fall Classic; baseball's postseason is notoriously unpredictable. But these teams won 98 and 103 games in the regular season, respectively, and led the AL and NL more or less wire-to-wire. They were the best in baseball, and they proved as much in October. Now it's time to see which will make history and capture their franchise's first-ever World Series title.
Full World Series schedule: Milwaukee will be rocking for Game 1
We'll have a few days of waiting: Game 1 is set for Friday, Oct. 23, with first pitch from American Family Field in Milwaukee at 8 p.m. ET. The series will follow the traditional 2-3-2 format, with days off for travel after Games 2 and 5. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be in Milwaukee, with Games 3-5 in Tampa.
| Game | Location | Date | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game 1 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 23 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 2 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 24 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 3 | Tropicana Field | Monday, Oct. 26 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 4 | Tropicana Field | Tuesday, Oct. 27 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 5 | Tropicana Field | Wednesday, Oct. 28 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 6 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 30 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 7 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 31 | 8 p.m. ET |
The Rays are grateful for the break, as it will allow them to reset their pitching staff and line ace Drew Rasmussen up to face off against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1. Clinching on Monday also allows Freddy Peralta to potentially get the ball in Game 2 on Saturday on full rest, with Nick Martinez likely behind him in Game 3.
Of course, the last thing the Brewers need is more rest. They clinched the NLCS in Game 4 last Thursday, Oct. 15, meaning they've already been at home for four days. By the time Game 1 of the World Series rolls around, it'll have been over a week since they last played a competitive game. Rust is overblown this time of year, but it's still something to monitor.
How to watch the 2026 World Series
This year's World Series will be broadcast exclusively on FOX.
- Dates: Oct. 23-Oct. 31
- TV channel: FOX
- Streaming: FOX One, YouTube TV, Hulu + Live Sports
You can also stream all the action on FOX One, provided you have a Fox One subscription ($19.99/month) or a valid cable login. You can also stream FOX through a variety of platforms, from YouTube TV to Hulu to Sling TV — all of which have free trials for new customers.
Pitching and power will define Brewers-Rays matchup
Suffice to say that runs are going to be at a premium in this series. Milwaukee ranked second in baseball in team ERA during the regular season, while the Rays were seventh. With Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and the best bullpen in baseball on one side and Rasmussen, Peralta, Martinez and All-Star closer Bryan Baker on the other, these teams have arms for days.
As such, it's going to be awfully hard to string together rallies — which means the team that finds a way to access some power will be at a distinct advantage. Neither team played much long ball during the regular season; both ranked in the bottom third of the league in homers, and neither ranked in the top 10 in slugging percentage. But the Brewers actually outslugged the big, bad Dodgers in the NLCS, and the Rays pulled away from Cleveland when their big bats (Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda) finally found the power stroke.
There won't be a ton of homers in this series. But whichever team has the most will almost certainly be hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy when all is said and done. If you're trying to play small ball against Abner Uribe, good luck.

item.title: [puckettspond.com] This year's World Series shows where the Twins have failed
item.dc:creator: Chris Schad
item.description: The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful. Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a s
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful.
Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night and they will face either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians in what will be a showdown between small-market teams.
While this year’s matchup could create a loophole for the Pohlad family to avoid dropping a large amount of money to improve the team, it also reflects poorly on their decisions that have kept them from competing over the past few years.
The Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing the Twins how to build a winner
As you may have guessed, the Brewers, Guardians and Rays are not among MLB’s biggest spenders. According to Cot’s Baseball Contracts, the Brewers’ year-end salary ranked 23rd at $99.3 million and defeated the Dodgers’ No. 1 roster at $366.0 million. The American League finalists were also budget-conscious as the Rays ranked 20th with a year-end payroll of $103.1 million and the Guardians ranked 25th at $91.0 million.
All three of the remaining teams had a lower year-end payroll than the Twins, who ranked 17th with a figure of $123.9 million and while many, including owner and chairman Tom Pohlad, believe that adding to that number could lead to a championship, the other three teams show what they have done wrong.
The first is maximizing the value of players on the roster. The Rays, Guardians and Brewers have traded players before they get to free agency to add to their organization and it’s paid off in a big way. The Brewers most notably did this in a February 2024 trade featuring Corbin Burnes that brought back left-hander DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz.
The Rays also have done this with their trade of Triple-A right-hander Tobias Myers, who was traded to Cleveland as he was eligible for the Rule 5 Draft in 2021, and brought back star third baseman Junior Caminero in return. While the Guardians whiffed on Myers, they made other shrewd deals that netted them Craig Yoho, Patrick Bailey, Foster Griffin and Kyle Manzardo.
These trades are a double-edged sword as they usually involve popular players. But it brings back pieces that ensure a larger championship window. That leaves player development as the final phase of the three contenders and each team has a homegrown star to lean on such as Jose Ramirez, Jacob Misiorowski or Caminero.
The Twins’ biggest problems go beyond their payroll
Turning the attention back to the Twins, it’s easy to see where they have come up short. This year’s trade deadline was one opportunity to shift the narrative. But instead of trading players that could bring back a big return such as Ryan Jeffers and Joe Ryan, the Twins went the opposite direction, adding A.J. Minter, Jeff Hoffman and Dean Kremer.
Even when they tried to trade Trevor Larnach to the Houston Astros before owner Jim Crane vetoed it, they were seeking 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, a pitcher who posted his highest ERA (3.73) and lowest WAR (1.0) since his rookie season in 2021.
The other key issue is the Twins’ player development. While top prospects such as Royce Lewis and Matt Wallner thrive initially when reaching the major leagues, those players have hit a wall when pitchers adjust to them. The problem can be traced back to Miguel Sano’s downfall in the early 2020s and can still be seen in a group of post-hype hitters that haven’t lived up to their prospect status.
This leaves the Twins in a tricky spot this offseason. After failing to trade Jeffers at the deadline, there’s a good chance he’ll leave in free agency. Ryan has a year of team control remaining, but trading him now could get a pair of MLB-ready players in return. Several top prospects including Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez and Kaelen Culpepper made their debuts this season, but the key will be to make sure they don’t regress entering their first full season in the bigs.
Of course, fans may cheer for a salary floor to hold the Pohlads accountable for what happens to the Twins next. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers show that paying top dollar may not be necessary to build a contender and Minnesota would be wise to follow their blueprint.

item.content:encoded:
Milwaukee Brewers superstar Jackson Chourio is the odds-on favorite to win the World Series MVP in the 2026 Fall Classic.
The Brewers advanced to the World Series for the first time since 1982, when they took down the mighty Los Angeles Dodgers, the reigning two-time World Series champions, with an eye-opening 4-0 sweep in the NLCS.
It was an absolutely incredible performance by the Brewers, who are now four wins away from capturing the first World Series championship in franchise history.
If they do end up winning it, then the oddsmakers like Chourio’s chances to be a big part of them doing so.
Jackson Chourio Is the World Series MVP Favorite
Per DraftKings Sportsbook, Chourio is the odds-on favorite to win the World Series MVP award this season.
Chourio is currently at +600 odds, putting him just ahead of his Brewers teammates, C William Contreras at +650, SP Jacob Misiorowski at +700, and 2B Brice Turang at +900, to capture this year’s World Series MVP award.
Since the ALCS between the Cleveland Guardians and the Tampa Bay Rays has not yet been decided, the odds will change from now until the start of the World Series one week from now.
Still, Chourio will be among the favorites to capture the World Series MVP award when the Brewers try to win the first championship in club history.
Jackson Chourio Is a Young Stud
Just 22 years old, Chourio is a young stud who has proven that he is one of the best young players in MLB since making his debut in 2024.
This season, Chourio hit .291 with a .837 OPS and a 129 OPS+ for the Brewers, indicating that his bat was 29% above league average.
He also belted 25 home runs and racked up 4.9 bWAR for the Brewers, along with stealing 23 bases.
Defensively, he had a strong year in LF and is a finalist for the Gold Glove Award.
During the postseason this year, Chourio has struggled a bit with just a .171 batting average, .553 OPS, and two home runs in eight games. But that is a very small sample size, and the oddsmakers know that he can turn it on at any moment.

item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray impressed in his first, and maybe only, season in Boston.
When the Boston Red Sox acquired Sonny Gray in an offseason deal with the St. Louis Cardinals, they were met with plenty of skepticism about whether or not the 36-year-old veteran could pitch in a big market like Boston after struggling during his time in New York as a member of the Yankees, and whether he could recapture his front-of-the-rotation form this late in his career. Those two questions he answered emphatically, posting one of the best seasons of his career.
In 29 starts for Boston, Gray posted a 2.72 ERA, the fifth-lowest among qualified American League starters and the eighth-lowest among qualified starters in baseball. In addition to posting the second-lowest ERA of his career, Gray finished the season tied for the league lead in wins with 18. Gray’s career renaissance was especially important in 2026, as the Red Sox lost 2025 American League Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet to a left shoulder injury on April 26, which ended his regular season. In Crochet’s absence, Gray and rookie Payton Tolle helped carry the Red Sox pitching staff to the third-lowest team ERA in baseball.
As a result of his career renaissance season, Gray has earned a nod of respect from his peers, being named one of the three finalists for the American League’s Most Outstanding Pitcher at the MLB Players’ Choice Awards. Gray is joined by New York Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and Toronto Blue Jays ace Dylan Cease. No surprises among the trio named finalists, as they could very well be the same three named finalists for the American League Cy Young Award.
After putting his name on the map with a dominant Game 3 performance against the Red Sox in the 2025 Wild Card series, Schlittler’s second act was somehow better than his postseason performance. In 33 starts for New York, the Walpole, Mass. native posted a 1.95 ERA, the lowest among all qualified American League starters and second-lowest among all qualified starters in the sport. His spectacular sophomore season is likely to earn him the AL Cy Young Award.
Cease posted an almost equally impressive first season in Toronto. In 29 starts, the 30-year-old right-hander posted a 2.40 ERA, trailing only Schlittler in the American League, and the fourth-lowest mark among all qualified starters in the sport. Cease also continued his run as one of the most prolific strikeout pitchers in the sport, punching out 12.73 batters per nine innings, leading the American League and trailing only Milwaukee Brewers ace and likely National League Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead.
The MLB Players' Choice Award winners will be announced during the week of Oct. 26.
Of note
With the Red Sox officially in offseason mode, Zach Coe and David Azer are back on the 'Entering Kenmore' Podcast discussing how close Boston is to winning a World Series, offseason needs, and whether or not the 2026 season was successful. Check it out wherever you get your podcasts, or in the YouTube player below:

item.content:encoded:
Get to Know Milwaukee Brewers Pitcher Jacob Misiorowski’s Fiancée
The Milwaukee Brewers are making a big postseason run, currently leading the Los Angeles Dodgers 3-0 in the National League Championship Series. If they win on October 15, they’ll head to the World Series for the first time since 1982.
The 24-year-old professional baseball team has a lot of players contributing to their success this season, including pitcher Jacob Misiorowski. This is just Jacob’s second season in the MLB and he’s having quite an incredible run.
Off the field, Jacob got engaged during his time off between the 2025 and 2026 baseball seasons. While he is mostly private about his relationship, we gathered everything we know so far. Scroll down for more.
Who is Jacob Misiorowski’s fiancée?
Since Jacob and Elle are so private about their relationship, very little is known about her. In a July 2026 interview, Jacob revealed that Elle played softball in high school and had an impressive arm.
“Jacob Misiorowski and his fiancé, Elle, might be the hardest throwing couple in baseball,” the reporter wrote on X. “He told me she was hitting the low 70s while playing softball as a catcher when they were in high school. Talk about a power couple!”
View this post on Instagram
Jacob follows one Elle on Instagram, Elle Nicas, but her profile is private. She became a fifth grade teacher at Matthews Elementary School in Grain Valley, Missouri, where Jacob is from, in July 2024.
Her employment was announced on the school’s Instagram with the following caption: “Ms. Nicas is excited to build relationships with students and to help them learn and grow. She is also excited to develop her skills and become the best teacher possible for her students. Ms. Nicas loves working in education because she loves seeing students grow throughout the year and creating activities tailored to her student’s interests.”
The pro athlete announced his engagement to Elle on January 12 with an Instagram post of her left hand showing off the engagement ring. He captioned it with a red heart emoji.
Of his proposal, Jacob told WISN it was “nothing too crazy” and that he “just asked the question.”
How did Jacob Misiorowski meet his fiancée?
Jacob and Elle seemingly met in high school. He attended Grain Valley High School in Missouri, and there was an Elle Nicas who played on the school’s softball team until she graduated in 2020. Jacob also graduated that year.
When is Jacob Misiorowski getting married?
When Jacob spoke to WISN in February 2026, he said his wedding to Elle was still “an offseason or two away,” which means he’ll likely get married in winter 2027 or winter 2028.

item.content:encoded:
An Outstanding first year as a Blue Jay 👨🏻 Dylan Cease is a Finalist for the @MLBPA’s Outstanding Pitcher Award!
Blue Jays’ Dylan Cease nominated for MLBPA’s outstanding pitcher award
Photo credit: John E. Sokolowski-Imagn Images
Dylan Cease’s 2026 greatness has been recognized among his peers. 
On Wednesday, Cease was recognized as one of three American League finalists for outstanding pitcher in Major League Baseball Players Association’s Players Choice Awards. Cease was nominated alongside New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler and Boston Red Sox right-hander Sonny Gray. 
Signed by the Toronto Blue Jays to a seven-year, $210-million contract on December 2, 2025, Cease did nothing but impress in his first season north of the border. Cease made 29 starts and went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA and a 1.10 WHIP. 
Cease struck out 239 batters – tied for third-most with Schlittler in Major League Baseball – and held opponents to a sparkling .180 average. The only pitcher in the majors who beat Cease’s mark of .180 was Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Jacob Misiorowski, who held opponents to a .157 average. 
The 30-year-old’s best month of the season came during July, when the right-hander made five starts and went 3-1 with a 1.00 ERA and 0.72 WHIP. Cease threw 36 innings and, during that span, struck out 46 batters and held opponents to a .125 average. 
Cease spent the month flirting with no-hitters, as on July 8, during a 10-0 win over the San Francisco Giants, the right-hander was three outs away from history before outfielder Heliot Ramos opened the bottom of the ninth with a leadoff single. 
Two starts later, on July 25, Cease turned in a pitching line of 9.0 IP, 1 H, 0 R, 0 ER, 3 BB, 12 K during a 6-0 win over the Boston Red Sox. Cease threw 120 pitches in the outing, in what could be one of MLB’s best pitching performances of the 2026 campaign. 
Unfortunately for Cease, he appeared to run out of gas in September. Following a start against the Texas Rangers on September 18, in which Cease allowed four runs (one earned) across 2.2 innings, it was announced he would head for imaging on his right shoulder. Five days later, Cease was placed on the 15-day injured list, ultimately ending his season. 
With no structural damage, Cease is expected to enter spring training healthy as he prepares for his second season with the Blue Jays.

item.content:encoded:
The NLCS resumes at Dodger Stadium on Wednesday, with the Dodgers looking to embark on a comeback down 2-0 in the series against the Milwaukee Brewers.
The top three in the lineup remain the same, as Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Teoscar Hernández hit in the top three spots. The middle of the lineup received an adjustment that comes as little to no surprise with how Shohei Ohtani and Will Smith have hit in the postseason.
Kyle Tucker moves up to cleanup in the starting lineup, the highest spot in the order he's been placed in this October. After a rough regular season, Tucker has found his stride at the plate at the bottom of the lineup, slashing .300/.391/.500 with a home run and two RBI over six games. Tucker has faced Milwaukee's Game 3 starter Robert Gasser twice in his career, collecting three hits across six at-bats including a home run.
Andy Pages has also impressed at the plate this postseason, turning the page on what was a historically awful title run at the plate last year. The 2026 All-Star has five hits across 20 at-bats, with his highlights being his go-ahead, two-run single in Game 4 of the NLDS and for getting the Dodgers on the board against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1 of the NLCS. Pages has gone hitless since his Game 1 RBI single, but he moves up to fifth in the lineup against Gasser, also the highest spot he's hit in the postseason this year.
The elephant in the room is Shohei Ohtani getting moved all the way down to sixth in the lineup. Ohtani was adamant about playing in Game 3, and Dave Roberts ultimately granted his wish.
"He's adamant he feels good enough to be in there. He's close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it," manager Dave Roberts said Tuesday just before the Dodgers workout at Dodger Stadium. "He was very convicted that he is onto something mechanically. He was adamant that he can help us. He's well enough to help us win a baseball game. So that's all I needed to hear."
Try as he might to will his way into the lineup, Ohtani has been a detriment offensively since hitting his final regular season home run on Aug. 18 in Denver, and he's carried that funk over the team's six playoff games slashing just .150/.261/.150 with zero RBI. Ohtani had never hit as low as second in the lineup until Game 3 of the NLDS, and it's the first time Ohtani is hitting sixth in the lineup since Sept. 19, 2020 back when he was with the Angels.
Will Smith has also struggled mightily this October, and he slides all the way down to seventh in the starting lineup. Miguel Rojas gets the start at third base over Max Muncy against the left-hander Gasser, and Tommy Edman gets the start at second base, rounding things out in the lineup. Blake Snell makes his first start since getting the ball for Game 2 of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Brewers get just enough off Tarik Skubal, draw first blood in NLCS Game 1 win
item.dc:creator: Maddie Lee

item.content:encoded:
First and foremost, the Dodgers wanted Tarik Skubal on their team. When they pursued him at the trade deadline, they saw him as the rare player who could improve their odds of winning a third straight World Series.
It didn't hurt that by acquiring him they prevented other postseason contenders, including the Milwaukee Brewers, from landing the two-time Cy Young Award winner. The Dodgers guaranteed that they wouldn't have to face him in October.
"I'm sure it's in the back of your head, the teams that are interested," president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Sunday before the Dodgers' 2-1 loss to the Brewers in Game 1 of the National League Championship Series. "Certainly not a driver, but not nothing either. As far as how happy I am, I am very happy it's Skubal versus Miz and not Miz and Skubal [for the Brewers] in the next two."
Read more: Dodgers struggle against Milwaukee Brewers pitching in NLCS Game 1 loss
That sentiment rang even truer when the Dodgers dropped Game 1 at American Family Field, despite forcing "Miz" — Jacob Misiorowski, the NL Cy Young favorite — out of the game in just 4⅓ innings, and despite having Skubal, who lasted five innings but gave up two runs in a fine effort, on their side.
In a role reversal, the Dodgers, who scored almost exclusively via the home run in the first round, pulled ahead with a pesky approach at the plate.
Designated hitter Shohei Ohtani opened the second inning with a four-pitch walk. Then Teoscar Hernández and Andy Pages hit opposite-field singles to move Ohtani around the bases and give the Dodgers a 1-0 lead.
Taking a similar "grind him out" approach to the one they deployed against Atlanta Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the division series, the Dodgers forced Misiorowski to throw 35 pitches in the inning — 10 alone to Kyle Tucker, who worked a walk.
By the third inning, Misiorowski's fastball velocity, which touched 104 mph, had dropped to double digits. And though the Dodgers didn't score again against him, they continued to rack up his pitch count. By the time he exited with one out in the fifth, it was at 94.
The Brewers, known for their peskiness, instead tied the game with one swing against Skubal. In the bottom of the fourth inning, Brice Turang got the barrel of his bat to an inside sinker and lifted it over the fence in left-center, into the Brewers bullpen.
If Turang, who went two for 16 in the NLDS, is heating up at the plate, that could be bad news for the Dodgers.
Though the Brewers have players who can hit home runs, they pulled ahead the next inning with a sequence more closely aligned with their identity.
Skubal walked Garrett Mitchell on five pitches. Brewers rookie Cooper Pratt moved him into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt. And then Luis Lara sent a ground-ball single through the middle of the infield to drive in the go-ahead run.
Skubal battled traffic to get out of the inning without giving up another run. But in such a tight game, that marked the end of his start.
The American Family Field atmosphere added an extra charge to the close contest. The home crowd was perhaps its loudest (until an ear-splitting cheer at the final out) when it took issue with a balk call against Misiorowski. It looked as if he had picked off Hernández to end the fourth inning, but Hernández instead was awarded second base.
That play still was seared into their collective memory when Dodgers left-hander Alex Vesia picked off Jack Bauers at first base. Brewers fans shouted "balk!" over and over.
The bullpens battled to a scoreless draw, the Dodgers' last stand falling flat after Tucker and pinch-hitting rookie Josue De Paula drew a pair of two-out walks against Trevor Megill. But the Brewers closer got Mookie Betts to fly out and end it, as the edge the Brewers gained against Skubal held.
The road doesn't get much easier for the Dodgers in Game 2, when they'll face right-hander Logan Henderson, who held them to one run in seven innings when the Brewers came to Los Angeles in August. But imagine if instead the Brewers had outbid the Dodgers and they had to go through Skubal first.
"It would look really different," manager Dave Roberts said Saturday. "What those guys do — they had the best record in baseball. Certainly when you're talking about a seven-game series, to see Tarik on the other side … the series would look a lot different."
This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times.

item.title: [MLB.com] Skubal loses steam second time through in NLCS loss to Brewers
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen
item.description: MILWAUKEE -- Tarik Skubal has been about as consistent as they come since being traded to the Dodgers this summer, but for the first time in eight postseason starts, the two-time Cy Young Award winner did not record an out beyond the fifth inning. In a highly anticipated matchup between two of the most dominant starters in baseball, the Dodgers fell to the Brewers, 2-1, after Skubal allowed two runs over five innings in Game 1 of the NL Championship Series on Sunday night at American Family Fiel
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- Tarik Skubal has been about as consistent as they come since being traded to the Dodgers this summer, but for the first time in eight postseason starts, the two-time Cy Young Award winner did not record an out beyond the fifth inning.
In a highly anticipated matchup between two of the most dominant starters in baseball, the Dodgers fell to the Brewers, 2-1, after Skubal allowed two runs over five innings in Game 1 of the NL Championship Series on Sunday night at American Family Field.
The Dodgers were able to chase the Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski -- this year's presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner -- with one out in the fifth inning, but Andy Pages' RBI single in the second was the only damage they managed against him.
It was a tale of two trips through the order for Skubal, who was dominant through his first three innings. He retired nine of the first 10 Brewers he faced, striking out six of them. Andrew Vaughn, who doubled in the second inning, was the lone baserunner he allowed in that span.
But the Brewers came to life when they saw him for a second time. To open the fourth inning, Skubal fell behind 2-0 to Brice Turang, then tried to get back in the count by painting the inside corner with a sinker. Turang launched the offering a Statcast-projected 384 feet to left-center, out of reach of center fielder Pages, to tie the game.
Skubal's command began to falter in the fifth inning, when he issued a leadoff walk to Garrett Mitchell. Gifted a free base, the Brewers played their style of baseball to take the lead. Cooper Pratt bunted Mitchell over to second, and Mitchell scored on a base hit up the middle from Luis Lara.
The Brewers loaded the bases on a Jackson Chourio single and a Turang walk, but Skubal was able to get William Contreras to fly out to escape the jam. Still, the stressful fifth inning raised Skubal's pitch count to 81, and he was lifted in favor of Alex Vesia for the sixth.

item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI — Tarik Skubal feels healthy, fresh and ready to take the ball for the Dodgers in Sunday’s NLCS opener. Speaking at Saturday’s workout in Milwaukee, he praised the Brewers’ lineup and the pitcher he will face, Jacob Misiorowski. He also explained the easygoing start-day routine that has caught his teammates’ attention. For Skubal, being himself and keeping the task simple are part of getting ready for a game like this.
Milwaukee makes pitchers earn it
Skubal sees a Brewers team that can win in several ways, with hitters who make pitchers work throughout the order.
“First off, it’s a very talented roster. I think they do a lot of things really well,” he said. “They pitch, they play defense, they run the bases, they hit with runners in scoring position. They control the zone really well. Their walk percentage is up there at the top of the big leagues, I think, one through nine. And they don’t strike out a lot.”
“It’s a really good baseball team. They play the game the right way. I’ve got a lot of respect for the guys over there, and obviously the manager, Murph. I’m a big fan of his.”
On the mound, Skubal knows he will have to get ahead and earn outs in the strike zone.
“You’ve got to match it when you’re on the mound. Do everything you can to get ahead and understand they’re not going to chase,” he said. “Sometimes you’ve got to beat them in the zone. I think it’s going to be a fun matchup.”
Finding his own routine
Max Muncy and Dave Roberts have both spoken about how easy Skubal is to talk to on the day he pitches. Earlier in his career, he tried following the example of older starters.
“You come up and see all the older guys and the way they go about things. Almost always, they all have headphones in. They don’t really talk to anybody, and everybody stays out of their way,” Skubal said. “You naturally think, ‘Okay, that’s what big leaguers do. This is what I’m going to do.’”
“I did that early in my career, and I found it to be pretty exhausting. I found myself mentally exhausted in the second or third innings of games. I’m like, ‘Why am I tired? I should be ready to go today.’”
An injury in 2022 gave him time to rethink that approach.
“When I got hurt in ’22, I decided enough is enough. I’m caring way too much about all the little things that don’t really matter and don’t really impact the game of baseball,” he said. “Making sure the music is the right setting, making sure it’s the right songs at the right times. You’re caring about all the wrong things, I think.”
“For me, it was more mentally freeing to take my headphones off and be who I am and interact with guys. As it gets closer to game time, you get ready to go, and you’re going to go out there and compete.”
“I want to be myself, and then I’ll lock in as the game gets closer.”
A clubhouse that welcomed him
Skubal said the Dodgers encouraged him to bring that same approach when he joined the club.
“They have a culture where they want guys to be who they are. Be your authentic self, and they’re going to appreciate you for whatever that is,” he said. “Every guy’s different. We’re all humans at the end of the day, and we all tick differently. They wanted me to be me. That was the message early on.”
Getting to know his teammates took time, along with learning how each of them works.
“That’s something I also value, how to get everybody else going and marching in one direction,” he said. “Understanding how to communicate, that stuff takes time.”
“The clubhouse is great. Obviously, a veteran group, but at the same time very welcoming to who I am. We both have the same goal in mind, and that’s to win a World Series. That starts with Game 1 tomorrow.”
Respect for Misiorowski
Skubal enjoys studying pitching, and Misiorowski has given him plenty to watch. Beyond the velocity, he admires the right-hander’s ability to throw strikes.
“His ability to command pitches at that velocity consistently, he consistently gets ahead,” Skubal said. “Obviously, the velocity is what it is, and the stuff and the shapes are what they are. But I think his walk percentage and walks per nine are about as impressive as anything he does.”
“He forces teams to beat him. That’s the mark of a really good starting pitcher, a guy who’s going to force lineups to beat you. He does all those things.”
“As a fan of the game, I’m a fan as much as I’m a player, it’s fun to watch him pitch. Tomorrow is probably going to be a different story, but what he does is very impressive.”
“The pressure is a privilege”
The expectations around the Dodgers suit Skubal’s own goals.
“The pressure surrounding the Dodgers, I think it’s all a privilege,” he said. “As an athlete, this is what you want to be in. You want to have an expectation to win. I have those same expectations as a player.”
“Keeping the game the game, going out there and competing and doing what I can to put my team in a position to win, I think, is important. In bigger moments, simplify. Be who you are and leave it all out on the field.”
“You can live with whatever result happens as long as you gave it everything you had out there. That’s what I ask of myself every time out.”
Asked about his workload and how he feels heading into this start, Skubal gave an encouraging report.
“I feel good right now; I feel fresh. I feel healthy. That’s all you can ask for at this time of year,” he said. “The body feels good. I feel like the ball’s coming out really well, and I’m able to execute pitches.”
He wants to stay on the mound, while trusting Roberts and the relievers when it is time to hand over the ball.
“You trust the manager, trust the plan they have, trust the guys in the bullpen,” Skubal said. “The bullpen we have here is also very talented and can give us an advantage later in the game. You’ve got to trust that stuff and also trust where the game is, the situation.”
“I’m excited to go.”

item.content:encoded:
How fast does Jacob Misiorowski throw? Inside Brewers ace's insane velocity and how he reaches triple digits originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Brewers are the true definition of a team and pride themselves on that, but they aren't without stars.
Jacob Misiorowski is poised to win the NL Cy Young Award in his first full season, which saw him morph from an erratic fireballer into a legitimate ace.
Misiorowski has plenty in his arsenal, but what makes him so intimidating is quite simple: velocity.
Here's a look at how fast Misiorowski throws and how he's rewriting MLB history.
How fast does Jacob Misiorowski throw?
Misiorowski averaged 100.6 MPH on his four-seam fastball in 2026, the highest mark of any starting pitcher, according to Baseball Savant. Only relievers Mason Miller (101.4) and Edgardo Henriquez (100.7) came in higher than Misiorowski.
In fact, Misiorowski's average velocity was 2.3 MPH higher than any other full-time starter. Pittsburgh's Bubba Chandler (98.3) is second to Misiorowski.
Velocity doesn't just extend to the fastball for Misiorowski. Among the 156 pitchers who threw at least 1,500 pitches in 2026, Misiorowski averaged the fastest cutter at 95.8 MPH, tied for the fastest slider at 91.8 MPH and finished second behind only Jared Jones with a 92.5-MPH changeup. Misiorowski's 88.0 MPH curveball easily led all starters.
All of that velocity results in an unbelievable leaderboard of fastest pitches from 2026, littered with the same name. Here's what it looks like.
MORE:Full Dodgers vs. Brewers NLCS schedule
Fastest pitches in 2026
Misiorowski threw 1,115 pitches of at least 100 MPH. Mason Miller, with 518, finished second, but the closest starter to Misiorowski was Bubba Chandler with 156.
To no surprise, the fastest pitches leaderboard from 2026 looks like this:
| Pitcher | Velocity | Date |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 105.5 | June 26 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.8 | Oct. 3 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.7 | July 26 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.6 | Oct. 3 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.5 | June 12 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.5 | July 26 |
| Ben Joyce | 104.5 | Aug. 15 |
| Edgardo Henriquez | 104.5 | Sept. 4 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.5 | Sept. 8 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.5 | Oct. 3 |
| Ben Joyce | 104.4 | Aug. 15 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.3 | June 26 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.2 | July 26 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.2 | June 12 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.2 | June 19 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.2 | July 26 |
| Jacob Misiorowski | 104.2 | Aug. 15 |
Misiorowski has thrown 15 of the fastest 18 pitches in 2026 and 27 of the 34 pitches that came in at 104 MPH or higher. The Brewers ace's 105.5 MPH pitch to Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 26 comes in just behind Aroldis Chapman's record of 105.8 MPH.

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE, WI—The Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers are set to renew their postseason rivalry in the National League Championship Series, meeting for the second consecutive year and third time since 2018. While Milwaukee dominated the regular-season series, Los Angeles has owned this matchup in October, sweeping the Brewers in the 2025 NLCS and eliminating them in seven games in 2018.
The Dodgers also swept Milwaukee in the 2020 Wild Card Series, giving them a perfect record in three postseason meetings. Los Angeles has reached the World Series every time it has faced the Brewers in October, winning two of those three trips. Milwaukee will look to change that history after earning home-field advantage with a 103-win regular season.
The clubs met seven times during the 2026 regular season, with the Brewers winning four games and the Dodgers taking three. Despite losing the season series, Los Angeles outscored Milwaukee 27-25, setting the stage for another competitive October matchup.
The first meeting came from May 22nd through May 24th in Milwaukee, where the Dodgers won two of three. After dropping the opener, 5-1, Los Angeles bounced back with an 11-3 victory behind Teoscar Hernández, who hit a three-run homer and drove in six runs. Yoshinobu Yamamoto then delivered seven innings of one-run ball in the series finale, while Andy Pages homered in a 5-1 Dodgers win.
Milwaukee responded when the teams met again at Dodger Stadium from August 13th through August 16th, winning three of four games. The Brewers rallied against Edwin Díaz in the ninth inning to take the opener, wasting a strong start from Roki Sasaki. The Dodgers evened the series the following day behind another quality outing from Yamamoto, with Pages and Tommy Edman homering in a 3-1 victory.
The Brewers took control from there, beating Los Angeles 4-1 behind six strong innings from Jacob Misiorowski before closing out the series with a 6-2 win. Logan Henderson held the Dodgers to one run over seven innings in the finale, while Milwaukee capitalized on defensive mistakes and bullpen struggles to secure the season-series victory.
Despite those results, the Dodgers enter the NLCS with reasons for optimism, particularly after hitting eight home runs against Atlanta in the NLDS. Max Muncy led the way with three, while Freddie Freeman added two as Los Angeles rediscovered its power after a quieter second half. Milwaukee, meanwhile, relies less on the long ball and more on a deep lineup that led the majors with a .258 batting average, .341 on-base percentage and 10.6% walk rate.
The pitching matchup could ultimately decide the series. Los Angeles boasts a formidable rotation led by Tarik Skubal and Yamamoto, both of whom delivered dominant starts against Atlanta. Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow add depth, giving the Dodgers an advantage in established starting pitching. Milwaukee counters with Jacob Misiorowski, who posted a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts during the regular season, but questions remain about his role in the rotation.
The Brewers have the edge in the bullpen, however, after posting the National League’s best relief ERA at 3.40. Closer Trevor Megill converted 30 of 33 save opportunities, while Abner Uribe and Milwaukee’s collection of left-handed relievers give manager Pat Murphy several reliable late-inning options. The Dodgers’ bullpen looked sharper in the NLDS, but sustaining that success against Milwaukee will be essential.
Milwaukee also has defensive and baserunning advantages, ranking among the league’s best in defensive runs saved and stealing 162 bases during the regular season. The Dodgers’ defensive lapses against Atlanta showed how costly mistakes can become in October, making execution especially important against a Brewers team that thrives on putting pressure on its opponents.
Still, Los Angeles has the postseason experience and star power to make another deep run. Dave Roberts continues to prove he can navigate October, and the Dodgers have repeatedly delivered in high-pressure moments against Milwaukee. The Brewers’ 103 wins and regular-season success make them a formidable opponent. Still, the Dodgers’ rotation, power potential, and postseason pedigree give them a path to a third consecutive NLCS victory.
The regular-season results suggest this rematch could be tightly contested. If Los Angeles gets length from its starters, capitalizes on scoring opportunities, and limits defensive mistakes, it has a strong chance to continue its October dominance over Milwaukee. The Brewers, meanwhile, will look to use their bullpen depth, athletic defense, and relentless offense to turn the rivalry in their favor finally.
Pitching Matchup
Game One: Tarik Skubal (LHP) (1-0, 1.50 ERA) vs. Jacob Misiorowski (0-0, 4.50 ERA)
Game Two: Yoshinobu Yamamoto (1-0, 1.29 ERA) vs. TBD (0-0, 0.00 ERA)

Who’s In & Who’s Out?
The Dodgers enter their National League Championship Series rematch against the Brewers with several injury concerns, headlined by infielder Miguel Rojas, whose availability remains uncertain as the team finalizes its postseason roster.
Rojas is dealing with lower left back and hip pain and remains day-to-day. He completed an “encouraging” workout on October 9th, according to manager Dave Roberts. However, the Dodgers are still determining whether the veteran infielder is healthy enough to make the NLCS roster. Given his postseason experience and defensive versatility, Rojas’ status will be one of the biggest decisions facing Los Angeles ahead of the series.
On the pitching side, right-hander Will Klein could provide a potential reinforcement if the Dodgers need additional bullpen depth. Klein has been sidelined with right elbow discomfort since landing on the injured list on August 1st before being transferred to the 60-day injured list on September 2nd. He has progressed to facing hitters and remains a possible option for the postseason.
However, the Dodgers are unlikely to have right-hander Blake Treinen available for the NLCS. Treinen suffered right shoulder inflammation while warming up in the bullpen on September 26th and was placed on the 15-day injured list the following day. Although baseball operations president Andrew Friedman has not completely ruled out a postseason return, Treinen is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 campaign, with a return more likely in 2027.
Beyond those immediate postseason concerns, Los Angeles has several pitchers whose recoveries are expected to extend into next season. Right-hander Gavin Stone, who is dealing with right shoulder inflammation, was placed on the injured list on March 22nd and transferred to the 60-day injured list on April 1st. He finished the Triple-A season on a rehab assignment with Oklahoma City and is expected to return in 2027.
Right-hander Jake Cousins is also targeting a 2027 return as he continues recovering from Tommy John surgery. He was placed on the injured list on March 24th and transferred to the 60-day injured list on April 1st, finishing the Triple-A season on a rehab assignment with Oklahoma City. Similarly, right-hander Ben Casparius remains sidelined with right shoulder inflammation after landing on the injured list on April 13th and being transferred to the 60-day injured list on May 18th. He also finished the Triple-A season on a rehab assignment and is expected to return in 2027.
The Dodgers’ remaining injured pitchers face longer-term recovery timelines as well. Left-hander Eric Lauer was placed on the 15-day injured list on September 2nd with left elbow inflammation before being transferred to the 60-day injured list on September 11th. He is ineligible to return before the end of the season and is expected to remain out until 2027.
Right-hander Brusdar Graterol’s timeline is less certain. Recovering from right shoulder and lower back surgeries, Graterol was placed on the injured list on March 22nd and transferred to the 60-day injured list on May 17th. He later shared on social media that he underwent a surgical procedure on his back, and no timetable has been established for his return.
Day-to-day (1): Miguel Rojas
10-day Injured List (0):
15-day Injured List (1): Blake Treinen
60-day Injured List (6): Jake Cousins, Gavin Stone, Ben Casparius, Brusdar Graterol, Will Klein, Eric Lauer
The Brewers will enter their National League Championship Series rematch against the Dodgers dealing with several injuries, including multiple pitchers who will miss the remainder of the 2026 season. While most of the club’s injured players are expected to return in 2027, right-hander Brandon Woodruff remains a potential option if Milwaukee makes a deep postseason run.
Woodruff has been sidelined since being placed on the 60-day injured list on July 5th, with his designation transferred on July 12th, due to a right shoulder capsule injury. The veteran right-hander was recently cleared by his shoulder surgeon to attempt throwing off a mound, leaving open the possibility of a return during the World Series. However, time is running short for him to work his way back into game shape. “I know the clock is ticking against me,” Woodruff said on October 3rd. “But I’m trying, that’s for sure.”
Milwaukee’s No. 2 prospect, infielder Luis Peña, is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season and much of 2027 after fracturing his left fibula while stealing third base on September 5th. He was placed on the minor league seven-day injured list on September 6th and underwent surgery on September 24th. With a typical recovery timeline of six to nine months, Peña is expected to return in 2027.
Left-hander Brian Fitzpatrick has been out since being placed on the 60-day injured list on June 6th, with his designation transferred on June 9th, due to a left UCL strain. After seeking a second opinion from Dr. Keith Meister, Fitzpatrick underwent Tommy John surgery on July 1st. He is expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season and is not projected to return until mid or late 2027.
Right-hander Quinn Priester was placed on the injured list on March 25th and transferred to the 60-day injured list on June 6th after being diagnosed with right neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. He underwent successful season-ending thoracic outlet decompression surgery in Dallas on June 22nd and is expected to be ready for the start of the 2027 season.
Left-hander Angel Zerpa has been sidelined since April 29th due to left forearm tightness. He was transferred to the 60-day injured list on May 31st and underwent season-ending Tommy John surgery in Dallas on May 11th. Zerpa is expected to miss the remainder of the 2026 season, with a potential return projected for early to mid-2027.

Misiorowski took the mound to begin the opening contest of the NLDS against San Diego, and the Brewers will turn to their ace again to begin their best-of-seven series against Los Angeles. item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Déjà vu all over again in Dodgers vs. Brewers NLCS rematch
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: Baseball postseason, for all of its unpredictability, has brought us the meeting of the two best teams in the sport to determine the National League representative in the World Series. Ahead of last season's NLCS, the angle of David versus Goliath was heavily played in virtually any analysis—it didn't help the more centered angle that the Dodgers steamrolled the Brewers on their way to a sweep. item.content:encoded:
Baseball postseason, for all of its unpredictability, has brought us the meeting of the two best teams in the sport to determine the National League representative in the World Series. Ahead of last season's NLCS, the angle of David versus Goliath was heavily played in virtually any analysis—it didn't help the more centered angle that the Dodgers steamrolled the Brewers on their way to a sweep. This time around it might not be that simple.
The similarities are evident, with the Brewers, yet again, having home-field advantage as a team that better maximized its skill set in the regular season, all while the Dodgers remain the favorites to advance, as was the case last season. Having said that, foolish are those who project a similar imbalance to that of the previous NLCS—the expectation of a more tightly contested series goes through pitching.
It may appear like a small factor, but the fact that both teams won their Division Series in four games means that Pat Murphy and Dave Roberts can line up their pitching in the ideal way for this Championship Series. And pitching is the great equalizer here, as both teams are stacked in that department and neither offense is currently hot enough to the point of putting into question the likelihood of a series dominated by elite pitching.
For all the talent on the mound for the Dodgers, the odds-on favorite to win the NL Cy Young pitches on the other side in Jacob Misiorowski. He is joined by the rookie Logan Henderson at the front end of a pitching staff tied with the Dodgers for the second-highest ERA+ in baseball. Last year's Brewers ace, Freddy Peralta, was good, not great, in the series against Los Angeles, and that applied to several key Brewers pitchers in order for the Dodgers to sweep the series in four without major offensive explosions.
With starting pitching on both sides able to dominate, the Dodgers have an advantage from last season's team in that the bullpen brings a much greater sense of reliability, not only in depth but also in the backend. We probably get the sense most fans will watch Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott, waiting for them to fail all the way until the hypothetical final out of the World Series—but they've done enough to earn Dave Roberts' trust, and the plethora of options behind them ready for a high-leverage spot if things go south isn't to be ignored.
Such emphasis on pitching is a must from the Brewers side because offensively, despite Jake Bauers' breakout campaign at first, the Dodgers still retain a heavy advantage, one that might even be currently underplayed ahead of the series. With little to no action from some of its top hitters, the Dodgers weren't brilliant, but they still got theirs in key spots against the feisty Braves. Last postseason, the Dodgers offense wasn't bombastic against Milwaukee, but it did enough to capitalize on strong pitching, while the Brewers' attack was nowhere to be found against elite Dodger starting pitching.
Second to last in regular-season homers and top five in stolen bases, the Brewers' offense's best course of action to put a dent in Dodger pitching is through generating action on the basepaths — putting the bat on the ball and pressuring a defense that has vulnerabilities (I won't name any names — Teoscar Hernández, cough, cough). It's nearly unfathomable to imagine Blake Snell or Tyler Glasnow escaping a five-walk outing with just one run against the Brewers like they did facing the Braves.
All season long, the National League has clearly proven to be the superior league. It's only fitting that the winner of the NLCS, whoever that is, will enter the Fall Classic as the favorite to win it all — the Dodgers in pursuit of a threepeat and the Brewers in search of their first title.
